stem:
A 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium carbonate 750 mg at night for 5 years with a steady-state trough level of 0.7 mmol/L. She attends her GP for a routine review. She is well, taking no other medications, with no recent illness. She drinks 2 standard drinks per week and does not smoke. Her last full blood count, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, eGFR, calcium, and TSH were taken 9 months ago and were within normal limits. She wants to know what monitoring she needs from now on while she remains on lithium.

She is not pregnant and is using long-acting reversible contraception.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Well, fine resting tremor of hands, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 0.7 mmol/L 9 months ago; eGFR 84 mL/min/1.73m2; TSH 2.1 mU/L; calcium 2.42 mmol/L; FBC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring schedule?

options.text: Annual lithium level with electrolytes and renal function only if symptoms of toxicity occur.
Lithium level every 3 months without further renal or endocrine monitoring needed during stability.
Lithium level, electrolytes, and TSH every 6 months without parathyroid hormone or calcium tested.
Lithium level every 3 months with annual electrolytes, calcium, and TSH long term while on therapy.
Lithium level, electrolytes, eGFR, calcium, and TSH every 6 months long term.

stem:
A 24-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg at night 12 weeks ago by the community mental health team. He has gained 4.5 kg, has settled positive symptoms, and is functionally improving. His baseline metabolic screen at initiation was: BMI 25 kg/m2, fasting glucose 5.0 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4 percent, total cholesterol 4.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.2 mmol/L, prolactin 320 mIU/L, ECG QTc 410 ms. He has no personal or family history of diabetes or cardiovascular disease and does not smoke. He drinks alcohol minimally.

He attends his community mental health appointment today and asks whether any tests are due.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C, weight 79 kg (up from 74.5 kg)
data_table.Examination: Well, no abnormal movements; abdominal girth increased; mood euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Baseline 12 weeks ago as listed in stem; no repeat bloods since starting olanzapine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring at this visit?

options.text: Repeat fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid panel, and weight; recheck waist circumference and blood pressure.
Repeat only fasting glucose and HbA1c at this 12 week visit because lipids change more slowly.
Defer metabolic monitoring until the 6 month review, focusing on symptom response in the meantime.
Repeat lipid panel only; defer fasting glucose and HbA1c until the 24 week visit later this year.
Repeat ECG, prolactin, and metabolic panel together with assessment for tardive dyskinesia today.

stem: A 45-year-old man started varenicline twelve days ago and stopped smoking on day eight. He has nausea after each evening dose but no vomiting, is eating normally, and wants to keep going.

data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, sleeping well, no abnormal dreams

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reduce to 0.5 mg twice daily and take doses after food
Stop varenicline and start a 21 mg nicotine patch tomorrow
Continue the current dose and add metoclopramide 10 mg as required
Stop varenicline and refer him to Quitline for behavioural support
Halve the dose and stop varenicline at the end of week four

stem:
A 29-year-old female accountant presents to your psychiatry clinic for a second opinion. She describes lifelong difficulty sustaining attention on tasks she finds tedious, frequent careless errors at work, chronic disorganisation, time blindness, and emotional dysregulation. School reports from age 8 documented inattention, daydreaming, and incomplete homework. She has no childhood hyperactivity. Self-report scales show ASRS v1.1 part A six positive items out of six, and the DIVA-5 confirms five inattention symptoms with childhood onset, persistence, impairment in two domains, and exclusion of other better explanations. Her PHQ-9 is 4 and GAD-7 is 6. She has no psychotic symptoms, no current substance use, and her ECG is normal. She drives 30 minutes daily for work.

She has read about treatment options and is asking what comes next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Well groomed, normal affect, no abnormal movements, normal cardiovascular and neurological exam
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 410 ms; TFTs normal; FBC and U+E normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial atomoxetine 40 mg daily for 6 weeks before considering any stimulant therapy as the first-line option.
Refer for structured cognitive behavioural therapy alone over 6 months before any consideration of medication.
Commence lisdexamfetamine 30 mg orally each morning, review in 4 weeks, and advise no driving during titration.
Trial methylphenidate immediate release 5 mg three times daily without driving restrictions because doses are small.
Defer treatment and reassess in 6 months because her PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores are too high for stimulant prescribing.

subtopic_detail: Exploratory ingestion of an adult antidepressant by a toddler
stem: A mother telephones your general practice. Her 13 kg two-year-old was found with his grandmother's dosette box about 30 minutes ago and one 25 mg amitriptyline tablet is missing. He is alert, playing and has vomited once.

data_table.History: Well child, no regular medicines, immunisations up to date
data_table.Reported observations: Alert and active, warm and well perfused

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Send him to an emergency department now for monitoring
Observe at home and review if he becomes drowsy
Give activated charcoal at home before transfer
Arrange a review in the practice in two hours
Arrange an electrocardiogram at a local clinic tomorrow

stem:
A 22-year-old man with a known diagnosis of schizophrenia is brought from his community accommodation by his case manager. Over 5 days he has progressively stopped eating, drinking, and speaking. On examination he is mute, holds postures imposed on him for over a minute (waxy flexibility), and shows echolalia when prompted. He has not eaten in 48 hours. He is on no current antipsychotic having stopped his depot 3 months ago because of side effects. He has no fever. His Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale score is 18. Bedside investigations have just returned.

The team is now planning treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 110/min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility, echolalia, posturing; no rigidity, no clonus; mildly dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: CK 320 U/L; creatinine 95 micromol/L; sodium 138 mmol/L; CRP 6 mg/L; urine drug screen negative; CT brain normal
data_table.Medications: Nil current; last paliperidone depot 3 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg intramuscularly as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge with reassessment at 30 minutes.
Restart paliperidone palmitate depot 100 mg intramuscularly today as first-line treatment of the relapse.
Refer for urgent electroconvulsive therapy without trialling a benzodiazepine challenge first.
Bromocriptine 5 mg orally three times daily targeting central dopamine receptor agonism over 7 days.
Olanzapine 10 mg orally now and reassessment at 24 hours of the catatonic features by the team.

stem:
A 27-year-old man is referred to your community mental health service. Over the last 3 years he has had two clearly defined manic episodes lasting 4 to 6 weeks with elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, grandiose delusions, and pressured speech, each requiring inpatient admission. Between episodes, in periods totalling over 12 months out of the last 3 years, he has had persistent auditory hallucinations of a derogatory commentary voice and persecutory delusions about being followed by ASIO, without prominent mood symptoms during that time. He is currently euthymic on valproate 1000 mg daily but still hears the voice. Substance use, organic causes, and recent stressors have been excluded.

The team is preparing his diagnosis and treatment plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, organised speech; reports persecutory belief about being monitored and ongoing voices
data_table.Investigations: FBC, U+E, LFTs, TFTs, B12, folate, and CRP normal; CT brain normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features confined to episodes of severe mania.
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, because psychotic symptoms persist outside mood episodes.
Schizophrenia with comorbid recurrent major depressive disorder rather than schizoaffective disorder.
Delusional disorder coexisting with bipolar I disorder, because the delusions are non-bizarre persistent.
Substance-induced psychotic disorder with recurrent affective episodes triggered by past stimulant use.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, two prior manic episodes (one with psychotic features), and two prior depressive episodes, has been stable on sodium valproate 1500 mg daily for 4 years with no episodes. She presents to your perinatal psychiatry clinic with a positive home pregnancy test today. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She had not been planning pregnancy. She is otherwise well, has no current mood symptoms, takes folate 500 micrograms daily, and lives with a supportive partner. She is well engaged with treatment, has private health insurance, and has no comorbid substance use. She is asking what to do about her medication.

Her most recent bloods are 2 months old.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, normal mental state examination; no neurological abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Bedside beta-hCG positive; pelvic ultrasound to be arranged; FBC, U+E, LFTs, and TSH 2 months ago all normal; valproate level 480 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1500 mg daily; folate 500 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at current dose because abrupt change risks a relapse during organogenesis.
Stop valproate abruptly today and reintroduce only if a manic relapse occurs during the pregnancy.
Cross-titrate valproate to quetiapine over 4 weeks, increase folate to 5 mg daily, and arrange dating scan.
Switch to lithium carbonate 750 mg at night during the first trimester then return to valproate later.
Add lamotrigine 25 mg daily to valproate, intending to taper valproate after the first trimester ends.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium 1000 mg nightly for 18 years with excellent mood stability. Her eGFR was 78 mL/min/1.73m2 two years ago and is 48 mL/min/1.73m2 today on a confirmatory repeat four weeks after the first reading. She has no acute illness, is well hydrated, and is on no nephrotoxic medications. Her ACR is 0.8 mg/mmol and renal ultrasound shows mildly bulky kidneys without obstruction. Latest lithium level 0.74 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8 mmol/L). She has had no manic or depressive episodes for 11 years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26, no peripheral oedema, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m2 (down from 78 two years ago), ACR 0.8 mg/mmol, lithium level 0.74 mmol/L, TSH 2.4 mU/L, calcium 2.36 mmol/L, renal ultrasound bulky kidneys without obstruction
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 1000 mg nocte for 18 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to nephrology and psychiatry to discuss switching from lithium to an alternative
Reduce lithium dose to 500 mg nightly and recheck eGFR in three months
Continue lithium unchanged and recheck eGFR every 12 months as usual care
Stop lithium abruptly today and start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily
Add amiloride to protect renal function and continue current lithium dose

subtopic_detail: Valproate in a woman of reproductive age
stem: A 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for three years after one severe manic episode. She attends review and tells you she has been in a new relationship for four months and would like to stop her copper IUD and try for a pregnancy in the next year. She has no current symptoms of mania or depression. She was previously intolerant of lithium (severe tremor at therapeutic levels) but has never tried other agents. She has no other medical conditions.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Mental state stable, no thought disorder, mood euthymic, no tremor
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 380 micromol/L (within therapeutic range), LFTs and FBC normal, beta-hCG negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate during conception and counsel on the 10% major malformation risk
Switch to lamotrigine before conception with gradual cross-titration and high-dose folate
Switch back to lithium and accept the previous tremor as cosmetic only
Stop all mood stabilisers preconception and restart only if a relapse occurs
Continue valproate and add quetiapine 300 mg nightly as additional cover

stem: A 27-year-old software engineer has been diagnosed by a psychiatrist with adult ADHD combined presentation. She has childhood symptoms documented in school reports, persistent inattention and impulsivity in adulthood, and significant occupational impairment. She has no history of cardiovascular disease, no substance use disorder, and no psychotic disorder. She has well-controlled generalised anxiety on sertraline 100 mg daily. She has a current Australian driver licence and her resting blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg with pulse 72.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Mental state alert and oriented, no thought disorder, mood mildly anxious but stable
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm rate 72, no QT prolongation, no LVH; baseline TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Methylphenidate immediate release titrated against effect and tolerability
Atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrated to 80 mg over four weeks as initial therapy
Long-acting lisdexamfetamine started at 30 mg daily and titrated weekly
Guanfacine extended release 1 mg daily titrated to 4 mg over six weeks
Bupropion 150 mg daily titrated to 300 mg over four weeks as monotherapy

stem: A 22-year-old man with first-episode psychosis is admitted to a psychiatric ward. Over 48 hours he becomes mute, immobile in a wax-flexible posture (he maintains an arm raised when positioned), and resistant to being moved. He has not eaten or drunk for 18 hours and his sodium is 134 mmol/L. He has been receiving risperidone 2 mg daily for four days. He has no fever, normal vitals, no rigidity, no autonomic instability, no rhabdomyolysis. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale screen is positive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility, posturing arm maintained when raised, no rigidity, no fever
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 134 mmol/L, creatine kinase 110 U/L (normal), Bush-Francis screen positive
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 2 mg daily commenced four days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently for electroconvulsive therapy without prior medication trial
Bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily with dantrolene for NMS suspicion
Continue risperidone and add diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily
Lorazepam 2 mg IV with reassessment of motor signs after 10 minutes
Start IV thiamine 300 mg three times daily for suspected Wernicke onset

stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought in by ambulance after deliberate ingestion of an unknown quantity of amitriptyline approximately three hours ago. She is drowsy but rousable, GCS 12 (E3V4M5), with dilated pupils and dry skin. She has had one generalised tonic-clonic seizure on arrival lasting 60 seconds that terminated after IV midazolam 5 mg. Pulse rate 124 sinus, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 37.4°C. Initial ECG shows sinus tachycardia with QRS 132 milliseconds and a terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 sinus, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 37.4°C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12, dilated pupils, dry skin, hyperreflexia, intact gag reflex
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 132 ms with terminal R aVR 4 mm; ABG pH 7.30, pCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L; paracetamol level negative
data_table.Medications: IV midazolam 5 mg given for seizure; IV access x2 with normal saline 500 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube as decontamination measure
IV flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to reversal of central anticholinergic effect
IV phenytoin 18 mg/kg loading dose to reduce TCA-induced seizure recurrence
IV lipid emulsion 20% 100 mL bolus then infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min
IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol bolus targeting QRS narrowing and pH 7.50-7.55

stem: A 24-year-old has had three discrete episodes over 18 months. Two episodes featured elevated mood with reduced need for sleep, grandiose delusions, and pressured speech for two weeks each, and resolved on a mood stabiliser. The third episode (most recent) featured persistent auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions for four weeks WITHOUT any mood symptoms before mood symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, hopelessness) supervened for the next three weeks. She has had no substance use, no thyroid disease, and a normal MRI brain. She is now stable on lithium and risperidone.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Currently euthymic, no thought disorder, no first-rank symptoms today
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mU/L, urine drug screen negative on multiple occasions, MRI brain normal
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg daily, risperidone 2 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features only
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type meeting full DSM-5-TR criteria
Schizophrenia with co-existing major depressive disorder of mild severity
Brief psychotic disorder followed by an unrelated major depressive episode
Substance- or medication-induced psychotic disorder ruled in on history

subtopic_detail: ECT consent and side effect counselling
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with severe melancholic depression and active suicidal intent has failed two adequate antidepressant trials and one augmentation. She is barely eating and has lost 8 kg in six weeks. The consultant psychiatrist has recommended a course of bilateral electroconvulsive therapy. She is competent to consent. She wishes to understand the most likely adverse effects before signing. She asks specifically about memory.

The registrar is undertaking the consent discussion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, flattened affect, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Bloods within normal limits; ECG normal sinus rhythm; CT brain normal
data_table.Medications: Mirtazapine 45 mg, lithium 750 mg/day, lorazepam 1 mg PRN

lead_in: Which adverse effect should be emphasised as the most common and persistent?

options.text: Memory impairment around the treatment period, usually improving in months
Permanent persistent global cognitive impairment in over half of patients
Brain damage with structural MRI changes after every treatment session
Cardiac arrhythmia with mortality risk above 1 in 100 sessions
Seizure threshold rise that always requires switching to ketamine anaesthesia

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is referred to the community mental health team with a two-year pattern of unstable mood, intense fear of abandonment, repeated self-cutting following arguments with her partner, two previous brief admissions following overdoses, and chronic feelings of emptiness. She meets DSM-5 criteria for borderline personality disorder. She has tried sertraline and quetiapine without sustained benefit. She is currently working part time. She has no current intent.

She asks what she should be offered now.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Multiple healed superficial forearm scars, mood reactive, no current intent
data_table.Investigations: Bloods within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment recommendation?

options.text: Structured DBT or mentalisation-based psychotherapy as primary treatment
Lithium 750 mg/day for affective instability as monotherapy
Long-term admission to a tertiary inpatient psychiatric unit
Increase quetiapine to 300 mg daily as long-term treatment
Cease all pharmacotherapy and offer supportive case management only

stem:
A 28-year-old presents with sudden left-sided weakness after a confrontation at work. Neurological examination shows give-way weakness, Hoover sign positive, and inconsistent power on distraction. MRI brain and cervical cord are normal. The patient appears distressed and concerned about the symptoms. There is no clear external incentive identified. She lives independently and is employed. She has no history of inconsistent presentations across hospitals.

The neurology team has referred for opinion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Give-way weakness left arm and leg, positive Hoover sign, inconsistent power on distraction
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and cervical cord normal; routine bloods within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder)
Malingering with an external secondary gain motivation
Factitious disorder with deliberate symptom fabrication for sick role
Acute ischaemic stroke not yet visible on early imaging
Multiple sclerosis presenting with first demyelinating event

stem:
A 31-year-old woman presents requesting assessment for autism. She reports lifelong difficulties with social interpretation, sensory sensitivities to noise and clothing, intense special interests in marine biology since childhood, and exhaustion after social interactions that she finds requires extensive preparation. She has high academic achievement and is employed as a librarian. She has previously been diagnosed with social anxiety and persistent depressive disorder. She scores 138 on the CAT-Q (camouflaging autistic traits). The GP letter notes apparent eye contact and conventional conversation in the consult.

The psychiatry registrar is reviewing referral options.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Mental state with appropriate but rehearsed-feeling social engagement
data_table.Investigations: AQ-50 score 39, CAT-Q 138

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for structured ADOS-2 plus ADI-R assessment by an experienced clinician
Reassure that adult diagnosis is not useful and continue treating social anxiety
Diagnose ASD based on the AQ-50 and CAT-Q screening results alone
Order genetic chromosomal microarray testing before clinical assessment
Start risperidone for autism-related symptoms before completing assessment

stem:
A 42-year-old man who arrived in Australia from Iraq four months ago presents to the GP with persistent headaches, body aches, palpitations, and disturbed sleep. He fled torture and incarceration in 2021. Through an interpreter, he says his head feels heavy and his chest feels tight. He cannot return to his country. He is supported by an asylum support service. He denies depressed mood when asked directly but reports nightmares and avoiding crowds. He is on a temporary protection visa.

A family member is in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: No focal neurology, cardiovascular and respiratory examinations within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, B12, ferritin, vitamin D within normal limits; ECG sinus rhythm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Professional interpreter (excluding family) and refugee trauma service referral
Reassure normal investigations and discharge with no further follow-up
Use the family member as interpreter to discuss trauma history
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg three times daily for ongoing anxiety
Refer to general adult mental health service without trauma-informed expertise

stem:
A 27-year-old man with schizophrenia, currently on a community treatment order, missed two depot appointments in the past month. His mother phones the community mental health team to report he is increasingly suspicious, not eating well, and has stopped his oral medications. He lives with his parents. He has not contacted the service. He has a history of two prior involuntary admissions following relapse during medication non-adherence. He has not been violent.

The registrar is determining the next clinical step.

data_table.Vital signs: Last recorded 6 weeks ago: pulse 78, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Last MSE 6 weeks ago: stable, well-engaged
data_table.Investigations: Last clozapine level 6 weeks ago therapeutic
data_table.Medications: Paliperidone depot monthly (last dose 5 weeks ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first action?

options.text: Urgent home visit (with police if safety risks) to assess under the CTO
Apply immediately for an inpatient involuntary treatment order without further assessment
Reassure the mother and wait until the next scheduled depot appointment in three weeks
Discharge the patient from the CTO since he has not contacted the service
Issue a breach notice under the CTO with no further clinical action this week

stem:
A 26-year-old man brought to the emergency department by police is shouting, threatening staff, and pacing in the assessment room. He has known schizophrenia and has had two previous similar presentations. De-escalation by an experienced clinician and an offer of oral medication have failed. He is detained under the Mental Health Act 2007 (NSW). He has no known cardiac history, weighs approximately 80 kg and has had no medication in the last 24 hours.

The team has the safe area set up and four trained staff present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 148/92 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Hyperaroused, pacing, shouting, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG and bloods not yet obtainable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first parenteral sedation?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg IM, with a second dose after 30 minutes if he has not settled
Olanzapine 10 mg IM together with midazolam 10 mg IM given as one regimen
Droperidol 10 mg IM, with a second dose after 15 minutes if he has not settled
Haloperidol 5 mg IM together with promethazine 25 mg IM given as one regimen
Ketamine 350 mg IM (about 4.4 mg/kg) as the first parenteral sedative

stem:
A 17-year-old presents with anorexia nervosa, restrictive subtype. Her BMI is 13.5 kg/m^2. She has lost 11 kg in three months. She has been eating around 600 kcal a day. Bloods: phosphate 0.6 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.6 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), albumin 28 g/L (35-50). ECG shows bradycardia with QTc 480 ms (normal less than 450). She is medically admitted overnight.

The paediatric and dietetic teams are planning refeeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38, BP 88/52 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 35.6°C
data_table.Examination: Cachexia, lanugo, cold peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.6 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.6 mmol/L, albumin 28 g/L, ECG QTc 480 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding plan?

options.text: 1400-1800 kcal/day with phosphate, potassium, magnesium, and thiamine cover
Start oral feeding at 500 kcal/day to avoid refeeding syndrome
Insert NGT and feed at full maintenance without electrolyte correction
Start IV dextrose 10% infusion without thiamine for rapid calorie delivery
Discharge home with weekly outpatient dietitian review only

stem:
A 22-year-old presented three months ago with first-episode psychosis precipitated by daily high-potency cannabis use. He was started on risperidone 4 mg and stopped cannabis at admission. His positive symptoms (persecutory delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations) have persisted despite three months of medication adherence and confirmed abstinence on urine toxicology. He has impaired functioning at university and social withdrawal. There is no family history of psychotic illness. He has not had a manic or depressive episode. No other substance use is identified.

The early psychosis team is reviewing the diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Flat affect, residual delusions of persecution, third-person hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Urine cannabinoid negative on three samples; routine bloods, MRI brain normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis at this stage?

options.text: Schizophrenia (cannabis was a precipitant in a vulnerable individual)
Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder, currently ongoing course
Brief psychotic disorder lasting longer than one month
Schizoaffective disorder, depressive subtype currently
Schizophreniform disorder still within the 6-month diagnostic window

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with a documented history of bipolar I disorder (one previous postpartum manic episode three years ago requiring inpatient care) has just delivered her second baby at 39+5. She stopped her lithium six months ago to plan pregnancy and has not restarted. On day 4 postpartum she is irritable, sleeping 1 hour per night, hyperverbal, has religious delusions about the baby, and is intermittently confused. She is breastfeeding. She is currently calm but the family are very concerned. She does not believe she is unwell.

The perinatal team has been called urgently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, religious delusions involving baby, intermittent confusion, MMSE 24/30
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH, calcium, magnesium, infection screen within normal limits; MRI brain not yet done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial step?

options.text: Admit to mother-baby unit, olanzapine 5-10 mg, lorazepam PRN, plus brain imaging
Restart lithium 250 mg twice daily and discharge with community follow-up
Reassure as normal postpartum baby blues and observe at home overnight
Cease breastfeeding immediately as a prerequisite to any medication
Initiate ECT same day before any pharmacological trial at all

stem:
A 28-year-old presents for a planning visit at 8 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She has had recurrent major depressive disorder for 6 years and has been well on sertraline 100 mg daily for 18 months. Two previous depressive episodes responded well to sertraline. She has had no manic or psychotic features.

She is unsure whether to continue medication. She has a supportive partner and a stable job. There is no recent suicidal ideation. Her partner is also concerned about possible fetal risks and asks for evidence-based advice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6 °C, fetal HR 160 bpm
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic, no psychomotor changes, normal reasoning, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods within normal limits; viability ultrasound shows single intrauterine pregnancy at 8 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication recommendation?

options.text: Switch to mirtazapine 15 mg nocte to avoid SSRI exposure to the fetus completely
Switch to paroxetine 20 mg daily for a smoother antidepressant profile in pregnancy
Cross-taper to fluoxetine 20 mg daily during the first trimester for safety reasons
Stop sertraline now and offer psychological therapy alone for the entire pregnancy
Continue sertraline 100 mg daily at the current effective antidepressant dose

stem:
A 38-year-old with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium carbonate 800 mg nocte for the last 4 years. Last week she developed acute gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhoea. She has continued her usual lithium dose and is now in your GP clinic with a mild tremor, mild ataxia, and slurred speech.

She has no other regular medications. Her last lithium level 3 months ago was 0.7 mmol/L on the morning trough (target 0.6-0.8). She has had no recent change in fluid or salt intake apart from the gastroenteritis and is mentally lucid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 90, BP 112/68 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, mild gait ataxia, dysarthria, no nystagmus, alert and orientated, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Bedside only, no lithium level drawn yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold the next dose, urgent serum lithium level and UEC at the same blood draw
Continue full-dose lithium and increase oral fluid intake to flush the drug through
Reduce the lithium dose by half empirically and review the patient in 2 weeks
Stop lithium permanently and start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily today
Refer immediately to the renal team for haemodialysis without measuring the level

stem:
A 22-year-old presents to the emergency department 90 minutes after ingesting approximately 50 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets in a suicide attempt. She is drowsy but rousable. She has had one self-terminating generalised seizure in the ambulance.

On arrival she is intubated for airway protection. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 130 bpm with a QRS duration of 130 milliseconds and a terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm. Bedside glucose is normal, paracetamol level is sent, and she has IV access in place.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130, BP 90/56 mmHg, RR 12 (ventilated), SpO2 98% on 40% FiO2, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Intubated and sedated, GCS prior to intubation 9, dry mucous membranes, sluggish pupils, hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia QRS 130 ms with aVR terminal R 4 mm, VBG pH 7.30 pCO2 38 mmHg HCO3 19 mmol/L (22-32), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), paracetamol pending
data_table.Medications: Currently nil; previously amitriptyline 25 mg prescribed for chronic pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg bolus, repeated every minute to reverse drowsiness
Intravenous physostigmine 1 mg bolus to reverse central and peripheral antimuscarinic effect
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated to a target QRS <120 ms
Intravenous activated charcoal 50 g via the nasogastric tube once airway is protected
Intravenous lidocaine infusion 1 mg/kg load then 1-4 mg/min for tachyarrhythmia control

stem:
A 28-year-old with schizophrenia has been on olanzapine 15 mg nocte for 8 months with full symptomatic remission. At his routine review you note he has gained 12 kg, his waist circumference is now 110 cm, fasting glucose is 6.5 mmol/L, and lipids show triglycerides 2.8 mmol/L and HDL 0.8 mmol/L. He is sedentary, eats takeaway most evenings, but does not drink alcohol.

He asks about whether his medication should change. He has had one previous relapse on quetiapine following self-cessation 2 years ago. He has no diabetes, no cardiovascular disease, and no extrapyramidal features.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: BMI 32 kg/m^2 (baseline 28), waist 110 cm, no EPS, no parkinsonism, no akathisia
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.4), HbA1c 6.0%, triglycerides 2.8 mmol/L (<2.0), HDL 0.8 mmol/L (>1.0), LDL 3.5 mmol/L, prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication strategy?

options.text: Cross-taper olanzapine to risperidone 4 mg mane to improve the metabolic profile
Reduce olanzapine dose to 5 mg nocte and continue current lifestyle advice only
Continue olanzapine at current dose and add metformin 500 mg twice daily for glucose
Cross-taper olanzapine to aripiprazole 15 mg morning while monitoring relapse risk
Switch to clozapine 12.5 mg daily titrated to maintenance dose with weekly bloods

stem:
A 26-year-old presents with a 6-week history of elevated mood, reduced sleep need, grandiose plans, and pressure of speech. During this time he believes he is being followed by ASIO operatives and hears their voices commenting on his actions. His mother says these psychotic features have persisted for 3 weeks now without any of the elevated-mood symptoms.

He has had two prior depressive episodes treated by his GP. He has no significant past medical history, no substance use, and no family history of psychosis. His thyroid function and urine drug screen are normal. There is no head trauma history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Currently mood euthymic, mild psychomotor slowing, persistent persecutory delusion, auditory hallucinations, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: TFTs within normal limits, urine drug screen negative, FBC and UEC within normal limits, MRI brain awaiting

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, current episode with manic features
Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, with mood-congruent psychotic features
Schizophrenia, paranoid subtype with comorbid recurrent depressive episodes
Major depressive disorder, current severe with psychotic features and mixed mania
Brief psychotic disorder with marked stressor lasting less than one month duration

stem:
A 26-year-old at 16 weeks gestation attends her GP for review. She smokes 15 cigarettes daily and has done so since age 17. She has tried unsuccessfully to quit during the first trimester using behavioural strategies alone. Her partner also smokes but is willing to support her quit attempt.

She has no other psychiatric or medical history, no significant past medical history, and is on no other medications apart from a pregnancy multivitamin. She asks specifically about pharmacological help because she feels behavioural advice has not been enough.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 °C, fetal HR 152 bpm
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic, no anxiety symptoms, no psychomotor changes, weight tracking on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods within normal limits, CO breath analyser 18 ppm (smoker range), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological option?

options.text: Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for one week then increased to twice daily
Varenicline 0.5 mg titrated daily for 12 weeks as the most effective oral agent
Intermittent nicotine replacement therapy by 2 mg lozenge as needed for cravings
Electronic cigarettes with 12 mg/mL nicotine for use throughout the pregnancy day
Continuous nicotine 21 mg patch for 16 hours daily across the next 8 to 12 weeks

stem:
A 24-year-old with a 2-year history of major depression presents to ED brought in by family. He has not spoken for 2 days, refuses food and water, and adopts unusual postures that he maintains for long periods. The family say he was started on no new medications recently and has not been on antipsychotics in the past.

On examination he stares without blinking, allows you to lift his arm into an unusual position which he maintains, and resists passive movement of his other limbs. His temperature is mildly elevated. There are no focal neurological signs. His urine drug screen is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 140/86 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 37.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mute, posturing with waxy flexibility, negativism, staring without blinking, no focal neurology, hydration moderate to poor
data_table.Investigations: FBC and UEC within normal limits, CK 320 U/L (<170), urine drug screen negative, CT brain unremarkable, lumbar puncture pending if no improvement
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg mane, no antipsychotic exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Mechanical ventilation and IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg for presumed malignant catatonia now
Bilateral electroconvulsive therapy under general anaesthesia within the next 24 hours
Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg with promethazine 25 mg for rapid behavioural control
Empirical IV ceftriaxone 2 g plus aciclovir 10 mg/kg for suspected encephalitis cover
Intravenous lorazepam 2 mg over 2 minutes with reassessment of catatonia at 15 minutes

stem:
A 38-year-old with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg nocte for 18 months with sustained remission of positive and negative symptoms. He attends his routine clozapine clinic. He has no fever, no infection, no mucositis, and feels his usual self. He takes no other regular medications.

His weekly FBC today shows a neutrophil count of 1.2 × 10^9/L (lower limit 2.0); his haemoglobin and platelets are within normal limits. Last week his neutrophil count was 2.3 × 10^9/L. A repeat FBC drawn 4 hours later in the same clinic confirms 1.2 × 10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No oral lesions, no rash, no infection focus, mental state stable, no positive or negative symptoms
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.2 × 10^9/L on repeat (2.0-7.5), Hb 142 g/L, platelets 280 × 10^9/L, CRP <5 mg/L, no infection focus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue clozapine but increase FBC monitoring to twice weekly with infection precautions
Stop clozapine immediately and refer to haematology for granulocyte colony stimulating factor
Reduce clozapine dose to 200 mg nocte and review FBC again in one week's time
Switch to olanzapine 20 mg nocte from tonight without further clozapine dose given
Admit immediately for IV broad-spectrum antibiotics until neutrophils recover above 2.0

subtopic_detail: Postnatal depression severity and treatment escalation
stem:
A 32-year-old woman is 8 weeks postpartum after a forceps delivery and prolonged second stage. She presents to her GP for the routine 6 to 8 week postnatal check, where she completes an EPDS that scores 18 out of 30, with positive endorsement of question 10 about "thoughts of harming myself have occurred to me" recorded as "sometimes". She describes a 4-week history of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep beyond the baby's feeding pattern, and decreased appetite with 3 kg weight loss. She is breastfeeding exclusively. She denies plans or intent to harm herself or her baby.

She has no prior psychiatric history and no history of bipolar disorder, postpartum psychosis, or postnatal psychiatric admission in herself or her family.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mood low, affect reactive but constricted, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no suicidal plans or intent on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: EPDS 18/30, item 10 positive (sometimes); TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), Hb 124 g/L (115-160), ferritin 28 micrograms/L (15-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg twice daily and continue to monitor
Commence fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily and recommend formula feeding
Refer immediately to mother-baby inpatient unit for admission
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily and refer for perinatal CBT
Refer for interpersonal therapy only and review in 2 weeks

subtopic_detail: First-episode psychosis - organic vs functional discrimination
stem:
A 22-year-old male university student is brought to ED by his parents with a 2-day history of new bizarre behaviour, paranoid statements that strangers are following him, and tactile hallucinations of insects on his skin. He has been recently treated with prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days for an asthma exacerbation, finishing 3 days ago. He has had no fever, no headache, no neck stiffness, and no overseas travel. His parents say he attended a music festival 1 week ago.

His usual medications include fluticasone-salmeterol inhaler and a recently completed prednisolone course. He has no other psychiatric history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Disoriented to date but oriented to person and place, fluctuant attention with inability to recite months backwards, mydriatic pupils 6 mm reactive bilaterally, dry warm flushed skin, no focal neurology, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: FBC and CRP within normal limits, UEC and LFTs within normal limits, MRI brain normal, urine drug screen pending, blood ammonia within normal limits, TSH within normal limits, B12 within normal limits, CT head normal
data_table.Medications: Fluticasone-salmeterol; recent prednisolone 50 mg/day for 5 days (last dose 3 days ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send urine drug screen for amphetamines, give lorazepam 1 mg IV, and observe quietly
Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg for HSV encephalitis pending lumbar puncture
Diagnose corticosteroid-induced psychosis and stop the prednisolone now
Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally and admit to psychiatry as first-episode psychosis
Discharge home with his parents and follow up with his GP in 1 week

subtopic_detail: Adolescent anorexia nervosa - refeeding syndrome risk and admission criteria
stem:
A 15-year-old girl is brought to ED by her mother. She has lost 12 kg over the past 6 months and has been restricting food intake to about 600 kcal/day. Her current BMI is 14.8 (below 0.4 percentile for age). She admits to compensatory exercise (running 10 km daily) but denies purging. She has had no menses for 5 months. She is medically stable on initial review.

Her mother is concerned and supportive. The adolescent eating disorder team has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42, BP 88/54 mmHg, RR 12, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 35.6 °C, postural BP drop 22 mmHg from lying to standing
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, dry skin, lanugo, cool peripheries, no proximal weakness, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Mg 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), phosphate 0.74 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), glucose 2.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), Hb 102 g/L (115-160), platelets 142 x10^9/L (150-400), LFTs ALT 86 U/L (<35), prolonged QTc 480 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with daily GP review and oral nutritional supplements
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily for comorbid depression
Commence olanzapine 5 mg orally daily for appetite stimulation
Refer to outpatient family-based therapy and review in 1 week
Admit for cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD pharmacotherapy with anxiety comorbidity and driving
stem:
A 28-year-old man is referred to a psychiatrist by his GP for new diagnosis of adult ADHD using DIVA-5 interview. He has a long history of inattention, distractibility, and forgetfulness. He works as a commercial truck driver and his employer requires fitness-to-drive review for the heavy vehicle category. He has co-existing generalised anxiety disorder partially controlled on escitalopram 20 mg daily. He has no history of substance misuse or cardiovascular disease.

His ECG and cardiology assessment have been completed by his GP.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic, mild restlessness, no tremor, no thyroid enlargement, no cardiac murmur
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal sinus rhythm with no QT prolongation, TSH within normal limits, FBC within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence long-acting methylphenidate after notifying medical assessor
Commence dexamfetamine 20 mg twice daily without medical assessor notification
Defer ADHD pharmacotherapy until he stops commercial driving altogether
Commence clonidine 50 micrograms orally twice daily as monotherapy
Commence atomoxetine 40 mg orally daily because of driving restriction

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with recurrent unipolar major depressive disorder has failed two adequate antidepressant trials: sertraline 200 mg daily for 8 weeks and venlafaxine XR 225 mg daily for 8 weeks. She remains moderately depressed with PHQ-9 score 16 and has lost 5 kg over the last 3 months. She has had no manic or hypomanic episodes and her sleep is initial insomnia with terminal early-morning waking. She is not psychotic. Her thyroid function is normal.

She is currently on venlafaxine 225 mg and has reasonable adherence. Her psychiatrist is reviewing options.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mood low, congruent affect, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, MMSE 30/30, no manic features ever
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), B12 within normal limits, ferritin 78 micrograms/L (15-200), Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), random cortisol within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Venlafaxine XR 225 mg daily (current trial 8 weeks)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily for symptomatic relief
Refer for psychodynamic therapy and stop venlafaxine immediately
Add aripiprazole 5 mg orally daily while continuing venlafaxine
Switch to a monoamine oxidase inhibitor with appropriate 2-week washout
Add St John's wort 900 mg orally daily as augmentation therapy

subtopic_detail: Legal authority to treat a catatonic patient who cannot consent in NSW
stem: A 47-year-old woman in Sydney with catatonia complicating bipolar disorder is mute and takes no food or fluid. She cannot take part in any discussion about treatment. Her sister asks you to treat her.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: mute, immobile, negativism; unable to communicate a treatment decision

lead_in: What is the most appropriate step?

options.text: Detain and treat her under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007
Take consent from her sister as the person responsible
Apply to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal first
Await a return of capacity before beginning any active treatment
Rely on common law necessity and document the discussion

subtopic_detail: Lithium toxicity at therapeutic level with NSAID interaction
stem:
A 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium 750 mg orally daily for 8 years is reviewed for new confusion, tremor and ataxia over the past 5 days. Her serum lithium concentration today is 0.85 mmol/L (target 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance). She has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for the past 10 days for shoulder pain prescribed by her GP. She also takes perindopril 5 mg daily for hypertension that was started 6 months ago.

Her last clozapine review documented stable mood for 3 years. She has no recent fever, vomiting or diarrhoea.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly drowsy, oriented to person, coarse postural tremor, broad-based gait with truncal ataxia, hyperreflexia, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.85 mmol/L (0.6-1.0), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 88), Na 138 mmol/L (135-145), TSH 4.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), CRP 6 mg/L (<5), urine output 30 mL/hour over 6 hours, ECG normal QT
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, ibuprofen 400 mg TDS (10 days)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch lithium to sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily
Refer for emergency haemodialysis to remove lithium urgently
Continue current lithium dose and reassess in clinic in 1 week
Restrict free water and add furosemide for renal recovery support
Stop ibuprofen and perindopril, hold lithium, give IV fluids, monitor serially

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis treatment escalation - ECT vs lithium
stem:
A 31-year-old woman is admitted to a perinatal mother-baby psychiatric unit 6 days postpartum following her first delivery. She has had 48 hours of severe insomnia, fluctuant mood between elation and confusion, paranoid persecutory delusions about strangers harming her baby, and command auditory hallucinations telling her to "get rid of" the baby. She is breastfeeding. The on-call perinatal psychiatrist has assessed her with the on-call consultant. She has a maternal aunt with bipolar disorder. The baby is being co-cared with her in the mother-baby unit with continuous staff oversight.

She has been started on olanzapine 10 mg orally nocte 48 hours ago with limited response and her delusions have intensified overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110, BP 134/82 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Disorganised speech, fluctuant mood, persistent delusions and auditory hallucinations, no fever, no focal neurology, no thyroid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: FBC within normal limits, UEC within normal limits, TSH within normal limits, B12 within normal limits, MRI brain not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 10 mg nocte (commenced 48 hours ago); paracetamol prn

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 20 mg nocte and observe for further 72 hours
Commence lithium 250 mg orally twice daily and discontinue breastfeeding
Add diazepam 10 mg orally three times daily for symptomatic relief
Refer to community mental health team for outpatient follow-up
Refer for urgent electroconvulsive therapy with continued co-care of the baby

stem:
A 46-year-old woman is reviewed in the community mental health clinic. She has a 14-year history of recurrent major depressive disorder. Her current episode has been ongoing for 11 months. She has previously had two adequate trials: sertraline 200 mg daily for 8 weeks, and venlafaxine XR 225 mg daily for 10 weeks with no significant response. She is currently 8 weeks into a third trial of escitalopram 20 mg daily plus weekly individual CBT with a clinical psychologist. There has been minimal change in her PHQ-9 score (19 baseline, 17 current).

She has no psychotic features and no suicidal plan. She is keen to add a medication rather than switch again. The psychiatry registrar has just completed a thorough history.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: PHQ-9 17/27, MoCA 28/30, no psychotic features, no manic symptoms past or present, no thoughts of self-harm, mild psychomotor slowing
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits; ECG QTc 410 ms
data_table.Medications: Escitalopram 20 mg daily (week 8), individual CBT weekly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Increase escitalopram to 30 mg daily as an off-label high-dose monotherapy trial
Add aripiprazole 2 to 5 mg daily as a PBS-listed atypical antipsychotic augmenter
Add diazepam 5 mg twice daily for the anxious-depressive features experienced
Switch to phenelzine after a 14-day SSRI washout to commence MAOI monotherapy
Refer for transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) as an alternative to drugs

subtopic_detail: Lithium chronic toxicity precipitated by ACE inhibitor
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with type 1 bipolar disorder has been stable on lithium carbonate for 14 years. Her most recent lithium level a month ago was 0.7 mmol/L. She has a recent diagnosis of hypertension; her GP started perindopril 5 mg daily 12 days ago. She also takes a topical NSAID gel intermittently for shoulder pain. Today her family bring her to the emergency department because she has been increasingly drowsy, has a fine coarse hand tremor, mild slurred speech, and vomited twice this morning.

She is rousable, oriented to person and place, and cooperates with examination. The ED registrar has just taken a focused history and noted the new ACE inhibitor.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, coarse intentional hand tremor, mild dysarthria, gait ataxic, no focal weakness, no nystagmus, no seizure activity
data_table.Investigations: Lithium level 2.1 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6-1.0), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 78), sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, ECG normal QTc, BSL 5.4
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte (long-term), perindopril 5 mg daily (12 days), topical diclofenac PRN, atorvastatin 20 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Continue lithium and add intravenous furosemide to enhance lithium renal excretion
Withhold lithium and give 50 mL of 50% dextrose for presumed hypoglycaemic cause
Stop lithium and ACE, give intravenous saline, and discuss haemodialysis with renal
Continue lithium at half the current dose and review lithium level in 7 days' time
Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally to bind any unabsorbed lithium dose

stem:
A 30-year-old woman presents to her GP with her 8-week-old son. She has been increasingly tearful since 2 weeks postpartum. She describes low mood most days, loss of pleasure, poor sleep beyond what is needed by the baby, intrusive guilt about being a bad mother, and intermittent thoughts that her baby might be better off without her. She has no specific suicidal plan and no thoughts of harming the baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding and wants to continue. Her partner is supportive but works full time.

She has no prior psychiatric history and no medication allergies. The community child-health nurse completed an EPDS yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tearful, slumped posture, slowed speech, mild concentration difficulty, no psychotic features, EPDS 18/30 (positive screen)
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.6 mIU/L, ferritin 28 microgram/L (15-200), B12 280 pmol/L, FBC normal, vitamin D 56 nmol/L
data_table.Medications: Iron and vitamin D supplementation since pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer for involuntary admission to a mother-baby unit under the Mental Health Act
Initiate fluoxetine 20 mg daily and advise cessation of breastfeeding immediately
Initiate diazepam 2 mg twice daily for anxiety symptoms alongside breastfeeding
Initiate sertraline 50 mg daily and refer for CBT or interpersonal psychological therapy
Watchful waiting alone with an Edinburgh postnatal depression scale recheck in 4 weeks

stem:
A 27-year-old engineering postgraduate is referred to the adult ADHD specialist clinic after a structured assessment by an ADHD-experienced psychiatrist (DIVA-5 plus collateral from a childhood school report). He meets DSM-5 criteria for combined-presentation ADHD with onset of symptoms before age 12. He has trialled 6 months of cognitive behavioural therapy with persistent functional impairment in his postgraduate study and partner relationship. He has no current alcohol or substance use disorder, no cardiovascular disease, no family history of sudden cardiac death, and his last cardiology screen ECG was normal.

He has no history of bipolar disorder, psychosis, or eating disorder. The psychiatrist plans to commence stimulant therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: No tics, no chorea, normal cardiac auscultation, normal weight and height, MoCA 30/30
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal sinus rhythm with normal QTc, FBC, UEC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological choice?

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily for 7 days then 80 mg daily as a non-stimulant alternative
Modafinil 200 mg in the morning as an off-label wakefulness-promoting alternative
Clonidine 50 microgram nocte titrated weekly as a non-stimulant alpha-agonist option
Bupropion 150 mg daily as a non-controlled antidepressant agent with ADHD evidence
Methylphenidate immediate-release 10 mg twice daily, transitioning to long-acting

subtopic_detail: Preventing manic relapse in schizoaffective disorder
stem: A 35-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, has had two manic relapses in a year despite taking olanzapine at an adequate dose, with adherence confirmed by the community mental health team and by dispensing records. She is euthymic today and has no psychotic symptoms.

data_table.Medications: Olanzapine daily for two years, no other psychotropics
data_table.Investigations: eGFR above 90 mL/min/1.73m2, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add lithium to the current olanzapine
Add sodium valproate to the olanzapine
Switch from olanzapine to quetiapine
Add a serotonin reuptake inhibitor
Add lamotrigine to the olanzapine

subtopic_detail: Severe postpartum psychosis with catatonic features
stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 woman is admitted to the mother-baby psychiatric unit on day 8 postpartum. She had been hyperactive, grandiose and not sleeping for 3 days from day 4, then developed disorganised speech and persecutory delusions on day 7. She was started on olanzapine 10 mg yesterday but overnight she became mute, refused food and fluids, and now lies motionless in bed. Her partner is distressed at the bedside. The baby is being cared for by the woman's mother on the unit.

She has no prior psychiatric history. She has a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder. The medical registrar has examined her with the consultant perinatal psychiatrist.

Cease serotonergic agents including linezolid, aggressive cooling and benzodiazepine sedation, and consider cyproheptadine

A 45-year-old man has been stable on lithium 1000 mg orally at night for bipolar I disorder for 8 years. He sees you in your general practice clinic for a routine review. He reports good mood stability, no recent episodes, and no relapse since titration in his 30s. He works full-time. He has hypertension treated with perindopril 4 mg daily and has been advised on adequate fluid intake and salt consistency. His lithium-level pattern has been stable at 0.7-0.8 mmol/L every 6 months.

On examination he is well, with no tremor and a normal mental state examination. His thyroid is non-palpable and there is no goitre. He has not been investigated for renal function in the past 12 months because of a missed appointment. Bloods sent today show creatinine 105 micromol/L (60-110), eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m squared (over 60), TSH 5.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free T4 13 pmol/L (10-22), serum calcium 2.45 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), serum lithium 0.75 mmol/L (0.6-1.2 therapeutic for maintenance). His last creatinine 14 months ago was 88 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 128/82 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No tremor, no goitre, normal mental state, well-perfused
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 105 micromol/L (60-110) up from 88, eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m squared; TSH 5.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), free T4 13 pmol/L (10-22); calcium 2.45 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); lithium 0.75 mmol/L (0.6-1.2)
data_table.Medications: Lithium 1000 mg PO nocte; perindopril 4 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop lithium and switch to sodium valproate as the long-term mood stabiliser irrespective of patient preference
Recheck thyroid function and renal function in 6 weeks, commence levothyroxine 50 mcg, and document creatinine trend
Increase lithium dose to 1250 mg orally at night targeting a serum lithium level of 1.0 mmol/L on maintenance therapy
Discontinue perindopril urgently as it is causing the renal function decline associated with the lithium dose
Reduce lithium dose to 500 mg at night without further investigation and arrange annual lithium-level review

stem:
A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on olanzapine 15 mg orally at night for 2 years. He attends your general practice clinic for routine review. He reports good adherence, no relapse, and no recent change in functioning. He gained 12 kg over the first 6 months on olanzapine and a further 4 kg over the past year. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and is not on lipid or glucose-lowering medication.

On examination his BMI is 33 kg/m squared. Waist circumference is 108 cm. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable. Bloods sent at booking today show fasting glucose 6.7 mmol/L (4.0-6.0), HbA1c 6.4% (under 6.0), triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (under 1.7), HDL cholesterol 0.9 mmol/L (over 1.0), LDL cholesterol 3.4 mmol/L (under 3.5), total cholesterol 5.8 mmol/L (under 5.5), ALT 38 U/L (under 35), TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.5-4.0). data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.7 mmol/L (4.0-6.0), HbA1c 6.4% (under 6.0), triglycerides 2.6 (under 1.7), HDL 0.9 (over 1.0), LDL 3.4 (under 3.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged, refer for dietitian and exercise physiology, and review metabolic profile in 12 months
Discuss switch from olanzapine to aripiprazole and add metformin for impaired glucose and weight management
Discontinue olanzapine immediately and substitute clozapine to manage the metabolic and weight gain trajectory
Refer for bariatric surgery without trial of antipsychotic switch or metformin therapy first
