A 24-year-old man with a 3-year history of schizophrenia is brought to your emergency department by his sister after 5 days of becoming progressively withdrawn. She says 'he hasn't eaten for two days, he just stares at the wall, and when I tried to move his arm it stayed where I put it'. He has been on risperidone 4 mg orally at night, with intermittent adherence. He had a brief similar episode 12 months ago that resolved spontaneously over 10 days.

On examination he is mute, sitting rigidly upright with his right arm held above his head. He maintains a position into which his arm is passively placed for over 1 minute (waxy flexibility). He grimaces but does not speak or follow commands. There is no tremor. He is afebrile and there is no rigidity beyond catatonic posturing. Bloods show CK 320 U/L (under 200), white cell count 6.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 4 mg/L (under 5), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), urea normal. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is 14.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 90, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility, posturing, no rigidity, afebrile, no tremor, no acute neurological focal signs
data_table.Investigations: CK 320 U/L (under 200), WCC 6.4 x10^9/L, CRP 4 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L; CT head no acute findings; LP not yet performed
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 4 mg PO nocte intermittent adherence

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge and admit for ongoing treatment
Increase risperidone to 6 mg at night and commence benzatropine for any extrapyramidal side effect emergence
Commence empirical IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin for any unrecognised encephalitis aetiology behind catatonia
Order electroencephalography first and defer any pharmacological treatment until non-convulsive status is excluded
Refer immediately for electroconvulsive therapy as the only definitive treatment of catatonia before benzodiazepine trial

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis with comorbid anxiety
stem:
A 32-year-old accountant attends your general practice clinic with a 2-year history of worsening concentration, difficulty completing tasks, and missed deadlines. He says 'I have to write down every step or I lose track, my desk looks like an explosion, and I keep losing my keys'. He has also had persistent worry about work performance, initial insomnia, and muscle tension for the past 18 months. School reports from age 8 describe a 'bright but disorganised' boy whose teachers commented on inattention and inability to sit still.

He drinks 4 standard drinks a week and does not use other substances. There is no mood instability, no psychotic symptoms, no recent head injury, and no thyroid history. Thyroid function is normal on bloods this morning. He scored 22 on the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (cut-off 14 for probable diagnosis) and 16 on the GAD-7 (cut-off 15 for moderate to severe anxiety). His worry is unrelated to specific objects and is generalised across multiple domains over more than 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Restless during interview, fidgety, frequent loss of train of thought; mental state otherwise unremarkable, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), normal FBC and UEC; ASRS-v1.1 score 22; GAD-7 score 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a long-acting stimulant such as lisdexamfetamine for adult ADHD pending psychiatry confirmation later
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily for generalised anxiety and review in 6 weeks before any ADHD work-up
Refer to a psychiatrist for adult ADHD assessment, treat anxiety with first-line measures in parallel, and discuss driving safety
Order an electroencephalogram and brain magnetic resonance imaging before any further behavioural assessment occurs
Provide cognitive behavioural therapy alone for both inattention and anxiety and review at 12 weeks for response

stem:
A 28-year-old G1P1 woman is brought by her partner to your emergency department on day 9 postpartum. He says 'she hasn't slept for three nights, she's saying the baby has been swapped at the hospital and the radio is sending her messages'. She has had no prior psychiatric history but her mother has bipolar I disorder. She gave birth to a healthy term boy by normal vaginal delivery; the postnatal period was uneventful initially.

On examination she is alert but tangential, with rapid pressured speech and labile affect. She describes the radio referring to her by name and intermittent visual perceptions of 'shadows changing shape'. There is no fever, no rash, and no neck stiffness. She is breastfeeding and her baby is in good health. There is no acute risk identified in the moment but she repeatedly asks 'are they going to take him away because he is the wrong baby?'. Bedside vitals are unremarkable; haemoglobin 124 g/L, white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L, CRP 4 mg/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, urinalysis clear.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Tangential, pressured speech, labile affect, delusional content (baby identity, radio referential), visual misperceptions; no neck stiffness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L (115-150), WCC 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 4 mg/L (under 5), TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), urinalysis clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily for severe postnatal depression and arrange community midwife visit tomorrow
Provide reassurance, schedule a 1-week postnatal follow-up review, and continue breastfeeding without pharmacotherapy
Refer urgently to a community mental health team for case management without inpatient admission at this stage
Admit to a mother-baby unit, commence olanzapine, and consider lithium with a breastfeeding shared decision
Arrange outpatient cognitive behavioural therapy for postnatal adjustment and review in 4 weeks at her next visit

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features
stem:
A 31-year-old man with a 6-year mental health history attends your community psychiatry clinic for diagnostic clarification. His parents say 'when he's high he doesn't sleep, he talks fast, he buys things he can't afford, and he hears voices then'. He has had four hospital admissions: two for manic episodes with psychotic features (delusions of being a religious prophet, persecutory voices) and two for major depressive episodes with mood-congruent psychosis. Between episodes he has been functioning at work part-time.

Review of his records confirms that during 2 distinct periods, each lasting 4 to 6 weeks between admissions, he experienced delusions of telepathic communication and persecutory auditory hallucinations without concurrent prominent mood symptoms (his mood was 'flat but not depressed' and energy was preserved). His insight is generally good now. There is no substance misuse. He is currently on lithium 900 mg at night, lamotrigine 200 mg daily, and risperidone 4 mg at night, and is in partial remission. He asks 'what is my diagnosis?'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic at presentation, no current psychotic features, MMSE normal, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-1.2), TSH 2.0 mIU/L (0.5-4.0), eGFR 84 mL/min/1.73 m squared
data_table.Medications: Lithium 900 mg PO nocte; lamotrigine 200 mg PO daily; risperidone 4 mg PO nocte

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features confined entirely to mood episodes and no inter-episode psychosis
Schizophrenia with mood episodes secondary to neuroleptic adverse effects and demoralisation
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type given prominent mood episodes and inter-episode primary psychotic symptoms
Delusional disorder mixed type with comorbid bipolar I disorder and substance use diagnostic complication
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type with documented psychosis lasting at least 2 weeks without prominent mood

stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic on her own initiative requesting an autism assessment. She says 'I've masked all my life and I'm exhausted and I can't keep doing it'. She describes intense restricted interests since childhood (collecting and cataloguing fossils for 18 years), sensory sensitivities (overwhelmed in supermarkets, prefers seam-free clothing), and significant social exhaustion after work meetings. She has had a long-term partner for 5 years.

She was a high-achieving student through school and university (engineering degree, GPA 6.9/7) and has held the same software engineering job for 3 years. She struggles with workplace small talk and has had two episodes of generalised anxiety (one in second year of university, one this year) treated with cognitive behavioural therapy. She does not meet criteria for current depression (PHQ-9 = 6). Her father has been described as having 'quirky obsessive interests'. She has no history of self-injurious behaviour and her speech and motor milestones were normal in childhood. Her workplace has just transferred her to a new open-plan office, and she has been having panic attacks in the bathroom.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, normal speech rhythm and prosody, brief intermittent eye contact, no abnormal movements
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 = 6 (not depressed), GAD-7 = 14 (moderate-severe anxiety), AQ-50 = 38 (above clinical threshold of 32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder and commence sertraline 50 mg daily with cognitive behavioural therapy referral
Reassure her that high-functioning autism is unlikely given her professional success and partnered relationship status
Refer to a specialist multidisciplinary diagnostic service experienced in adult autism in women for formal assessment
Refer to occupational health for workplace accommodation under the Disability Discrimination Act before any diagnosis
Initiate intranasal oxytocin trial for autism social cognition difficulties as the first-line pharmacological intervention

stem:
A 51-year-old man presents to your general practice clinic for help quitting smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes per day for 33 years (pack-years over 40) and has tried unsupported quitting three times. He says 'I really want to stop for my grandkids, but I'm worried because I've been on antidepressants forever'. His major depressive disorder is currently in remission on sertraline 100 mg daily; the last episode was 2 years ago. He scores PHQ-9 = 3 today.

He has stable angina on metoprolol 25 mg twice daily and an ejection fraction of 60% on a recent echocardiogram. He has had no acute coronary syndrome in the last 12 months. He has no history of seizures, alcohol use disorder, or eating disorder. His BMI is 24. He has no suicidal ideation now and no past suicide attempts. He has tried nicotine replacement therapy in two of his prior attempts; he found the patch helpful but discontinued because of vivid dreams. He scores Fagerstrom = 7 (high dependence). Spirometry is mild obstruction (FEV1 78% predicted) with reversibility.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 64, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, no acute distress, mild expiratory wheeze on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 = 3 (remission); Fagerstrom = 7 (high dependence); FEV1 78% predicted with reversibility
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily, metoprolol 25 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily increasing to 150 mg twice daily after 1 week with target quit date in week 2
Combination nicotine replacement therapy patch plus lozenge as needed with behavioural support and weekly review
Nortriptyline 25 mg daily titrated to 75 mg as a TGA-approved off-label smoking cessation aid for resistant cases
Clonidine 0.1 mg twice daily as the AU first-line cessation aid in a patient with comorbid hypertension and depression
Varenicline starting 0.5 mg daily titrating to 1 mg twice daily over week 1 with quit date day 8 of treatment

stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to your community mental health team for the third time in 6 months after intentional superficial cutting of her forearm. She says 'when my boyfriend pulls away I feel like I'm disappearing and only the cutting brings me back'. She has chronic feelings of emptiness, recurrent self-harm without suicidal intent, intense unstable relationships, and rapidly shifting mood states. She has been on three different SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine) over 2 years without sustained benefit.

She has had two brief admissions for self-harm in the last year; she finds inpatient settings escalate rather than calm her. There is no current suicidal plan or intent. There is no current depression by PHQ-9 (= 9, mild). She uses cannabis on weekends and drinks 4 standard drinks twice a week. Her sleep is fragmented. She has no psychotic features and her reality testing is intact. Her family environment in childhood was emotionally invalidating with intermittent neglect; there is no formal trauma history at this assessment. Her GP has been prescribing repeat low-dose quetiapine 25 mg as needed for distress, which she uses two or three times a week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, mood labile, no psychomotor agitation, no thought disorder, multiple superficial healed forearm cuts
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 = 9 (mild), no current suicidal plan or intent; AUDIT-C = 4
data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 25 mg as needed (used 2-3 times per week); previously sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restart escitalopram 10 mg daily and titrate to 20 mg over 4 weeks aimed at chronic emotional dysregulation
Admit to an inpatient unit for at least 2 weeks of structured behavioural therapy and medication review
Increase the as-needed quetiapine dose to 100 mg with broader availability for breakthrough distress
Refer for structured psychological therapy (dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation-based therapy) with clear crisis plan
Commence lamotrigine 25 mg titrating to 200 mg over 8 weeks for affective instability in personality disorder

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features
stem:
A 26-year-old man is admitted to your inpatient psychiatry unit on an involuntary order. His sister says 'he's been hearing voices on and off for nearly a year now, even when he's not high or low'. His mood has alternated between two clear depressive episodes (3 and 7 months ago) and one clear manic episode (4 months ago, lasting 2 weeks with reduced sleep, grandiosity, hypersexuality, and pressured speech). Through this period he has had persistent auditory hallucinations of two male voices commenting on his actions, including at least 2 weeks of euthymia between episodes when the voices continued.

He has no substance use disorder. Urine drug screen is negative. There is no medical cause identified on workup (CT brain normal, TSH normal, B12 normal, syphilis serology negative, HIV negative). He has been started on olanzapine 10 mg with reasonable effect on the active psychotic symptoms and was previously on sertraline (currently off it). His insight is limited but improving. The family asks 'what is it actually, doctor?' and his sister insists 'he's not just bipolar'.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, cooperative, third-person auditory hallucinations described, normal speech rhythm, no thought disorder, mood currently euthymic
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, CT brain normal, TSH 1.8 mU/L (0.5-4.0), B12 410 pmol/L (200-700), HIV and syphilis negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features confined to mood episodes only and mood-congruent themes
Substance-induced psychotic disorder with mood symptoms secondary to long-standing cannabis dependence
Major depressive disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features in the context of repeated severe episodes
Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type with mood and psychotic symptoms in defined temporal relationship
Schizophreniform disorder with associated mood disturbance from social and occupational consequences of psychosis

stem:
A 19-year-old university student is admitted to your psychiatry unit with a 4-week history of paranoid delusions (his housemates are spying on him through air vents), third-person auditory hallucinations, and thought broadcasting. His mother says 'he's been smoking strong skunk weed almost every day for the last 2 years'. He has been continuously using high-potency cannabis (estimated 16% THC) daily for 24 months. Urine THC and metabolites are positive on admission.

He was abstinent for 4 weeks during a remote bushwalking trip 6 months ago; his mother says the voices and paranoid ideas continued throughout that abstinent period and only briefly faded when he returned and started using again. His paternal uncle has schizophrenia. He has had functional decline over 12 months (left first-year engineering after one semester) and his negative symptoms (amotivation, social withdrawal, blunted affect) have persisted for 8 months. There is no acute mood episode (PHQ-9 = 7, YMRS = 3). His insight is poor.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, paranoid, third-person auditory hallucinations, thought broadcasting, blunted affect, no abnormal movements
data_table.Investigations: Urine THC and metabolites positive, urine other drugs negative, CT brain normal, TSH normal, B12 normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder that will resolve with abstinence and supportive care alone
Schizotypal personality disorder with eccentric thinking exacerbated by chronic cannabis exposure
Brief psychotic disorder with substance-related precipitation expected to resolve fully within 4 weeks
Major depressive disorder with cannabis use complicating mood and producing transient pseudo-psychotic features
Primary schizophrenia (cannabis use as risk factor) with characteristic features sustained through abstinence

subtopic_detail: ECT in pregnancy with capacity and consent intact
stem: You are the consultation-liaison registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman at 24+3 weeks gestation with severe depression and active suicidal ideation. She has had no oral intake for 5 days and has lost 4 kg in 10 days. Four adequate antidepressant trials have failed and three previous ECT courses produced remission. Her capacity is documented as intact and she consents to ECT in writing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 99% room air, fetal HR 152 bpm
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 24, albumin 28 g/L, urea 9.2 mmol/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer ECT until after delivery and augment vortioxetine with quetiapine
Proceed with ECT using left lateral tilt and continuous fetal monitoring
Apply to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for an ECT administration inquiry
Start lithium augmentation as the first-line approach in refractory pregnancy depression

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is admitted to your psychiatry inpatient unit after 4 days of progressive withdrawal, mutism, and stillness at home. Her father says 'she's stopped talking, she just stares at the wall, and she's keeping her arm in whatever position I put it in'. She has a history of bipolar I disorder and stopped olanzapine 3 weeks ago against medical advice. She has not been febrile or autonomically unstable.

On examination she is awake but unresponsive to voice. She has waxy flexibility (your hand-placed arm remains in position for over 30 seconds), mutism with no spontaneous speech, posturing of the right arm above her head, and echopraxia of your face-touching gesture. She has no fever, no rigidity, and no rhabdomyolysis (creatine kinase 124 U/L, under 200). Her observations are stable. Bedside finger-prick glucose is 4.6 mmol/L. CT brain is normal. CSF is normal. White cell count is 7.4 x10^9/L (4-11). She has had no antipsychotic exposure in the last 3 weeks. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score is 14 (above the diagnostic threshold of 2 for catatonia present, with severity threshold of 8).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Awake, unresponsive to voice, waxy flexibility, mutism, posturing of right arm, echopraxia, no fever, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 14, CK 124 U/L (under 200), CT brain normal, CSF normal, WCC 7.4 x10^9/L (4-11)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone pulses for presumed autoimmune encephalitis with catatonic features
Administer a single intravenous lorazepam 2 mg bolus and observe for clinical response over the next 5-10 minutes
Restart olanzapine 10 mg orally as the primary management with concurrent supportive care
Commence electroconvulsive therapy as the first-line treatment without prior benzodiazepine trial
Trial intramuscular dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg as initial pharmacotherapy for presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome

stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for the last 3 years. She has had no manic or depressive episodes since starting valproate. Before this she had two hospital admissions for mania, both requiring inpatient stabilisation. She is in a stable relationship and her partner is also her primary carer.

She attends today to tell you that she and her partner are planning to start a family and would like to try to conceive within the next 6 months. She is using the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her latest valproate level is 78 mg/L (50-100), full blood count, liver function and weight are within normal limits, and she has had no significant tremor or hair thinning. She takes no other regular medication. Her older sister has bipolar I and conceived on lithium without complications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic; affect appropriate; no thought disorder; no psychomotor abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 78 mg/L (50-100); FBC, LFT within normal limits; BHCG negative; weight stable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate at the same dose but add folic acid 5 mg daily from preconception
Switch from sodium valproate to lithium with cross titration over 6 to 8 weeks before conception
Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily to lower exposure and continue through pregnancy
Switch to lamotrigine 200 mg daily as a mood stabiliser before conception planning
Stop valproate immediately with no alternative pharmacotherapy and offer psychological therapy alone

stem:
You are the ED registrar at a metropolitan tertiary hospital reviewing a 24-year-old woman brought in by ambulance one hour after an intentional ingestion of approximately 30 tablets of amitriptyline 50 mg, taken with vodka. She was found by her partner who called triple-0 immediately. She had been taking amitriptyline for migraine prophylaxis. She has no other regular medications and no significant past medical history.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable to voice. Pupils are 6 mm and sluggish. She has dry warm skin and absent bowel sounds. Her airway is patent but she cannot protect it if any further deterioration occurs. The ECG performed on arrival shows sinus rhythm at 118/min with a QRS duration of 132 ms and a terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm; the QTc is 480 ms. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, base excess -8. She is currently haemodynamically stable with a blood pressure of 102/64 mmHg but the ECG was repeated 10 minutes later and the QRS is now 142 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5); pupils 6 mm sluggish; dry warm skin; absent bowel sounds; airway patent
data_table.Investigations: ECG: QRS 132 ms then 142 ms over 10 min; aVR terminal R 4 mm; QTc 480 ms; pH 7.28; base excess -8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg for CNS depression from any co-ingested benzodiazepine
Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg via nasogastric tube and observe with cardiac monitoring
Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g for torsades prophylaxis given QTc 480 ms
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg and prepare for definitive airway control
Defer all therapy until a serum amitriptyline level returns to guide management severity

stem:
You are the on-call psychiatry registrar reviewing a 15-year-old girl in the ED who was brought in by her mother after she discovered superficial cuts to her forearm. The cuts were made with a kitchen knife two hours ago, are 1 to 2 mm deep, did not require sutures, and the mother is now waiting in the cubicle. She is in Year 10 at a local high school and is normally a good student.

She is reluctant to talk in front of her mother. When asked privately she discloses she has been cutting for the past three months as a way to cope with overwhelming feelings since her parents separated. She denies any current plans for suicide and does not have a plan or means in mind. She has had occasional fleeting thoughts that life is not worth living when very distressed but has not made any preparations. She has not used any substances. She does not own or have access to firearms. She is willing to engage with follow up and her mother is supportive.

You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman on the general medical ward referred for unresponsiveness for the last 48 hours. She has a 10 year history of recurrent major depression with two previous hospitalisations, currently on mirtazapine 30 mg nocte. Two weeks ago her GP added quetiapine 50 mg nocte for sleep and ruminations. She lives alone and her daughter brought her to the ED when she found her on the couch in the same position from the previous day.

On examination she is mute, eyes open but unblinking, lying immobile in bed. She does not respond to verbal stimuli. When you raise her arm above her head it remains in position for over a minute (waxy flexibility, positive Bush Francis catatonia rating). The medical team have excluded infection (clear CXR, normal urine, normal CRP), electrolyte derangement (sodium 138, calcium 2.32), thyroid disease (TSH normal), and a non contrast CT head and CT venogram are within normal limits. She has no fever and is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile, waxy flexibility positive; Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 14; no fever; no rigidity; no tremor
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138 mmol/L; calcium 2.32 mmol/L; TSH within normal limits; CRP <5 mg/L; CT head and venogram within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease mirtazapine immediately and start fluoxetine 20 mg as antidepressant rotation
Administer intravenous lorazepam 1 to 2 mg challenge and reassess in 10 minutes
Start dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV given suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome from quetiapine
Arrange urgent EEG to exclude non-convulsive status epilepticus before any treatment
Refer immediately for electroconvulsive therapy with 3-times-weekly bilateral sessions

A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends your general practice for cardiac rehab follow up six weeks after an inferior STEMI managed with primary PCI to the right coronary artery. He has been smoking 25 cigarettes a day for 40 years and was unable to quit on his own after his admission, although he has cut down to 12 a day. He has no history of depression, psychosis, suicidality or seizures. He is currently on aspirin 100 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, perindopril 5 mg, metformin 1 g twice daily and empagliflozin 10 mg.

His cardiac rehab clinician sent him to discuss pharmacotherapy options. He is highly motivated to quit before his upcoming holiday in three months, has tried nicotine patches alone twice in the past without success, and his wife is supportive. His BP today is 128/78 mmHg and pulse 72/min. He has no liver disease, no psychiatric history, and his eGFR is above 60 mL/min. He asks which medication is most likely to help him quit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No respiratory or cardiovascular signs; weight 92 kg; BMI 30
data_table.Investigations: eGFR >60 mL/min; LFTs within normal limits; HbA1c 6.6%; lipids on target

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement: 21 mg patch daily plus 4 mg lozenge as needed for 12 weeks
Bupropion 150 mg orally daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for 9 weeks total
Varenicline with the standard week 1 dose escalation then 1 mg twice daily for 11 weeks
Nortriptyline 75 mg orally nocte titrated upwards as a third line off-label cessation aid

You are the GP registrar at a community refugee health clinic seeing a 34-year-old woman who arrived in Australia six months ago on a humanitarian visa from a country of recent armed conflict. She lives with her three children in resettlement housing. She presents with sleep disturbance, intrusive flashbacks of the conflict, hypervigilance and avoidance of news media for the last 4 months. She speaks limited English and is accompanied by a female accredited interpreter she has worked with before.

She denies current suicidal ideation. She drinks no alcohol and does not use substances. She has no past psychiatric history. She is medically well; her physical examination is unremarkable. Her PCL-5 (administered with the interpreter using a validated translation) scores 52. She is reluctant to take medication and asks what other options exist. The clinic has access to a trauma-trained psychologist who works with an interpreter and a community-based peer support program for women from her language group.

data_table.Mental state: Hypervigilant; affect anxious; thought form linear; no psychotic features; insight preserved; PCL-5 score 52
data_table.History: Refugee from recent conflict; 6 months in Australia; safe housing; no current suicidality; no substance use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line intervention?

options.text: Refer to community peer support program alone without psychological therapy
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and titrate up over 4 weeks before therapy referral
Prescribe quetiapine 50 mg nocte for sleep and hypervigilance before specialist review
Recommend supportive counselling and watchful waiting given recent resettlement

You are the ED consultant called to assess a 47-year-old man with treatment-resistant depression brought in by his wife with confusion and agitation that began over the last 12 hours. His regular medications are escitalopram 20 mg, mirtazapine 30 mg and olanzapine 10 mg nocte, all stable for 6 months. Three days ago his GP added tramadol 50 mg three times daily for back pain. He has been increasingly restless, with shaking of all four limbs.

On examination he is agitated and diaphoretic. Pulse is 132/min, BP 168/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min and temperature 39.3 °C. Lower limb reflexes are markedly hyperactive with sustained ankle clonus bilaterally; upper limb reflexes are also brisk. There is intermittent myoclonus of the lower limbs. Pupils are 6 mm and reactive. Tone is increased in the lower limbs more than the upper limbs but there is no lead-pipe rigidity. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. CK is 980 U/L. He has been on this antipsychotic regimen without change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 168/96 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 39.3 °C
data_table.Examination: Agitated, diaphoretic; lower limb hyperreflexia with sustained ankle clonus bilaterally; myoclonus lower limbs; tone increased LL > UL, no lead-pipe rigidity; hyperactive bowel sounds; pupils 6 mm reactive
data_table.Investigations: CK 980 U/L (<200); WCC 11.4 x10^9/L; sodium, urea, creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start IV ceftriaxone and perform lumbar puncture for presumed acute meningoencephalitis pathway
Cease olanzapine and start IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Administer paracetamol 1 g for fever and arrange psychiatric admission for medication review
Give oral bromocriptine 2.5 mg and stop olanzapine immediately for presumed neuroleptic syndrome
Cease serotonergic agents, give IV crystalloid, start IV midazolam, admit to a cardiac-monitored bed

A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents to your psychiatry clinic for pre-conception counselling. She has been stable on lithium 800 mg nocte for 5 years with a serum concentration consistently 0.8 mmol/L; recent renal function and TSH are normal. She had three depressive recurrences and two manic episodes before lithium was started, with two psychiatric admissions during her teens. She has been well for the last 2 years and is in a stable partnership. She and her partner are now planning to conceive within 6 months.

She has read online that lithium is teratogenic and is considering stopping it before pregnancy. She has not had a recent mood relapse and her last quetiapine prescription was 4 years ago. She has no history of alcohol or substance use, body mass index is 24 kg/m2, blood pressure 118/70, and she is taking folate 5 mg daily. She has no thyroid or renal disease, no cardiac history, and her parents and siblings have no congenital heart disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 118/70 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic, no psychomotor change; insight preserved; BMI 24
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.8 mmol/L; creatinine 68 micromol/L; TSH 1.6 mIU/L; calcium within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Lithium 800 mg nocte for 5 years; folate 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Stop lithium during first trimester and resume in second trimester to avoid cardiac teratogenicity
Continue lithium with frequent serum monitoring and detailed fetal cardiac ultrasound at 20 weeks
Switch from lithium to sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily prior to conception for tighter mood stability
Switch to lamotrigine 200 mg daily prior to conception with slow titration and rash monitoring
Cease lithium prior to conception and manage prophylactically with no medication during pregnancy

stem:
A 24-year-old man was started on olanzapine 10 mg nocte 4 weeks ago for a first episode of psychosis following review at your early psychosis intervention service. He is now responding well; positive symptoms have reduced and he has returned to part-time work. He has gained 3 kg over the last month, has a normal appetite and reports no sedation that he notices. He continues to live with his parents.

On review his blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 76, body mass index 27 kg/m2. There is no extrapyramidal sign, no akathisia, and his insight is intact. He has not used cannabis or alcohol since starting treatment, smokes 5 cigarettes a day with intent to quit, and has not started any other medication. There is no family history of diabetes or cardiovascular disease. He asks what investigations should be done to look after his physical health while on the medication. His baseline fasting glucose, lipids, prolactin and ECG before starting olanzapine were all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 128/82 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: BMI 27; no extrapyramidal signs, no akathisia; insight intact
data_table.Investigations: Baseline fasting glucose, lipids, prolactin and ECG within normal limits 4 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate physical health monitoring plan?

options.text: Repeat baseline lipids and fasting glucose only if metabolic symptoms develop in the next 12 months
Fasting glucose and lipids monthly for the first 6 months then every 3 months indefinitely
Weight at every clinic visit; fasting lipids and glucose at 12 weeks then at 12 months and yearly
Haemoglobin A1c only at 6 months as the single marker of glucose intolerance during treatment
Oral glucose tolerance test at 3 months and again at 12 months as the gold standard test

A 52-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department by his wife with confusion since this morning, three days after stopping all alcohol prior to a planned elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He has been drinking 1 litre of spirits daily for 15 years with previous detoxification attempts that he did not complete. He has not eaten well for 2 weeks because of biliary pain. He has had two prior unwitnessed seizures that he attributes to alcohol withdrawal.

On examination he is disoriented to time and place with visual hallucinations of small insects on the wall. He has coarse tremor of the outstretched hands, diaphoresis and gait ataxia when assisted to stand. There is horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze in both directions. He is afebrile and there is no focal neurology. Capillary glucose is 4.8 mmol/L. The on call medical registrar has just confirmed sodium 138, potassium 3.4, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L and an ethanol concentration of 0 mmol/L. The bedside CIWA score is 24.

data_table.Examination: Disoriented, visual hallucinations, coarse tremor, diaphoresis, gait ataxia, horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze; CIWA 24
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.8 mmol/L; sodium 138, potassium 3.4, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L; ethanol concentration 0 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Mechanical restraint with observation while observing for self-resolution within 12 hours
Intravenous haloperidol 5 mg with maintenance of glucose 5% infusion plus oral thiamine 100 mg daily

A 35-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg daily for 6 months through your community early psychosis service. He has had a good clinical response with reduction in auditory hallucinations and stable mood. He attends today for his routine 4-weekly full blood count as required by the Australian Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service.

He reports no fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, or other infective symptoms; he denies any recent travel and remains a non smoker. His weight has been stable; he is up to date with vaccinations and lives with supportive parents. There has been no change in medication apart from a recent course of amoxicillin clavulanate for an upper respiratory tract infection 3 weeks ago. Today's full blood count comes back from the laboratory while he is still in the waiting area: white cell count 3.4 x10^9/L, absolute neutrophil count 1.2 x10^9/L (1.5-7.0), haemoglobin 142 g/L, platelets 198 x10^9/L. His previous monthly counts have all been within the green range.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Asymptomatic; no fever, sore throat or mouth ulcer; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: WCC 3.4 x10^9/L; ANC 1.2 x10^9/L (1.5-7.0); Hb 142 g/L; platelets 198 x10^9/L; prior monthly counts all within green range
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 400 mg daily for 6 months; recent amoxicillin clavulanate course completed 3 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add lithium 600 mg nightly to stimulate neutrophil production and continue current clozapine dose
Continue clozapine at the same dose and recheck the full blood count in 7 days as outpatient
Subcutaneous filgrastim 5 mcg/kg daily to support neutrophil count and continue clozapine therapy
Reduce the clozapine dose by 50% and recheck the full blood count in 48 hours
Cease clozapine immediately, recheck full blood count every 48 hours, and notify CPMS today

A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance at 3am with severe agitation, anxiety and tremor. He discloses that he has been using gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB) every 4 hours around the clock for the last 6 months and that his last dose was 18 hours ago. He works in a hospitality role and uses GHB to manage anxiety and to stay awake.

On examination he is agitated and diaphoretic. He is alert with tactile hallucinations of insects crawling on his skin. There are no focal neurological signs. Capillary glucose is 5.4 mmol/L. The senior emergency consultant has just confirmed he has had a normal ECG, normal CT brain, sodium 138, potassium 4.1 and a negative ethanol concentration. Lorazepam 2 mg intravenously was given 30 minutes ago without any reduction in agitation, and a further 2 mg given 10 minutes ago has not helped. He continues to attempt to leave the department.

data_table.Examination: Agitated, diaphoretic, tactile hallucinations; no focal neurology; CT brain normal
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal; sodium 138, potassium 4.1; ethanol negative; glucose 5.4 mmol/L; 4 mg IV lorazepam in last 30 minutes with no response

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous midazolam 5 mg now and titrate with further 5 mg doses every 5 minutes to settle agitation
Oral baclofen 10 mg three times daily for 7 days and discharge home with general practitioner review
Intravenous propofol 50 mg loading then 1 mg/kg/hour infusion without intubation or airway support
Restart oral GHB at the patient's home dose and titrate down over 7 to 10 days with regular review
Intravenous haloperidol 5 mg now for rapid behavioural control and continued observation in ED

A 32-year-old man with schizophrenia diagnosed at age 21 is reviewed in your community mental health team clinic. He has had persistent auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, and functional impairment for the last 18 months despite full adherence to medication. Six months ago he completed an 8 week trial of risperidone 6 mg daily at his therapeutic concentration after a 6 week trial of olanzapine 20 mg daily at therapeutic plasma concentration. Both trials confirmed dose, plasma level and adherence using SafeScript and pharmacy fill data.

He lives with supportive parents and is engaged with his case manager. There is no current substance use, no head injury, and a recent normal magnetic resonance imaging of the brain. Routine biochemistry, full blood count and ECG are normal. PANSS positive subscale today is 28 with prominent third person hallucinations and persecutory delusions; PANSS negative is 22. He is not actively suicidal but is socially withdrawn. He and his family agree that current medication is not working and are open to further treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Engaged with reviewer; third person auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions; PANSS positive 28, negative 22
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods, FBC, ECG within normal limits; MRI brain unremarkable; SafeScript and pharmacy fills confirm adherence to trials
data_table.Medications: Current risperidone 6 mg daily at therapeutic concentration for 8 weeks; prior olanzapine 20 mg daily for 6 weeks at therapeutic plasma concentration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological strategy?

options.text: Add lithium 600 mg nocte to current risperidone for augmentation of positive symptoms over 8 weeks
Initiate clozapine with mandatory CPMS registration and weekly full blood count monitoring
Add aripiprazole 15 mg orally daily to current risperidone for dopamine partial agonist augmentation
Switch to long-acting paliperidone palmitate 156 mg intramuscular monthly with adherence support
Switch to bilateral electroconvulsive therapy three times weekly for 12 sessions in an inpatient setting

A 28-year-old woman has been admitted to the acute mental health inpatient unit for 5 days with severe melancholic depression. Over the last 48 hours she has become mute, immobile in bed, refuses food and fluids, and waxily resists passive limb movement. She remains awake with eyes open but does not engage. There has been no recent medication change, no fever, no infective symptoms, and there is no history of substance use.

On examination her Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score is 18, with mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing and negativism present. She is now declining oral intake completely. Initial workup shows normal full blood count, normal urea and creatinine, normal calcium and magnesium, normal thyroid function, normal CK and a normal non contrast CT brain. EEG shows no epileptiform discharges and no encephalopathic pattern. A lorazepam challenge with 2 mg intravenous lorazepam every 4 hours has been used for 48 hours without any clinical change. She has lost 3 kg over the admission and the medical team is concerned about refeeding risk.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Bush-Francis 18; mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing, negativism; declines oral intake
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, calcium, magnesium, TFTs, CK and CT brain within normal limits; EEG no epileptiform or encephalopathic pattern; 48-hour lorazepam challenge (2 mg IV 4-hourly) without clinical response
data_table.Medications: IV lorazepam 2 mg 4-hourly for 48 hours with no change

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase lorazepam to 4 mg intravenously every 6 hours and observe for response over 72 hours
Sodium amytal interview to differentiate functional from organic catatonia before ECT consideration
Commence bilateral electroconvulsive therapy three times weekly with consent from substitute decision maker
Intravenous clozapine commencement with monitoring of full blood count weekly for 18 weeks
Intravenous haloperidol 5 mg twice daily for psychomotor retardation while continuing lorazepam

subtopic_detail: Severe lithium toxicity with renal impairment
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a tertiary ED reviewing a 56-year-old woman with bipolar disorder on lithium 1000 mg daily for 20 years. She reports 3 days of diarrhoea and vomiting from a presumed gastroenteritis and now feels weak and confused. Her usual lithium level a month ago was 0.8 mmol/L with normal renal function.

On arrival she is drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12. There is coarse tremor of both upper limbs, marked dysarthria, and broad-based ataxic gait when standing. She is on no other psychotropic medications and the family deny intentional overdose. Her recent regular bloods show baseline eGFR of 68 mL/min. The toxicology registrar has been contacted.

options.text: Immediate haemodialysis with planned 6-8 hour session and recheck level after rebound
Intravenous 0.9% saline at 1 L per hour with repeat lithium level every 4 hours
Activated charcoal 50 g orally plus intravenous 0.9% saline at 250 mL/hour
Cease lithium, observe in the high-dependency unit, recheck level in 24 hours
Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol solution via nasogastric tube

He is currently on 300 mg per day and has had a 3 day history of malaise, low-grade fever, and a new sense of mild shortness of breath. His last clozapine therapeutic drug monitoring was within range and the haematology monitoring shows an absolute neutrophil count of 4.2 x10^9/L.

On examination he describes mild left-sided chest discomfort that is worse on inspiration. He is mildly tachycardic at rest with no peripheral oedema. He has no risk factors for pulmonary embolism, no recent travel, no infective contacts, and no clinical signs of an upper respiratory tract infection. data_table.Investigations: ANC 4.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); clozapine TDM within range two weeks ago; no recent troponin or echocardiogram

options.text: Continue clozapine; prescribe paracetamol and arrange GP review in 48 hours
Cease clozapine; perform troponin, ECG, CRP, BNP and transthoracic echocardiogram

subtopic_detail: ECT for an involuntary patient with capacity who refuses
stem: A 67-year-old woman is an involuntary patient in a NSW mental health facility with psychotic depression. She is mute, immobile, and has been observed maintaining unusual limb postures for over an hour. Examination reveals waxy flexibility and intermittent grimacing. She has not eaten or drunk in 48 hours and has had no exposure to antipsychotic medication. She presented initially with disorganised speech and anxiety which then progressed to her current state.

This morning her temperature has risen to 38.4 °C and her creatine kinase is elevated. Neurology and infectious diseases have been consulted. Brain MRI yesterday was unremarkable. CSF cell count, glucose, and protein were normal but anti-NMDA receptor antibodies have been sent and are pending. The team is asking what to do next while waiting for those results.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Mute, immobile; waxy flexibility; sustained limb posturing; intermittent grimacing; reduced oral intake 48 hours
data_table.Investigations: CK 1800 U/L (40-200); FBC and electrolytes within normal limits; brain MRI unremarkable; CSF cell count normal; anti-NMDA receptor antibody result pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Intravenous haloperidol 5 mg as antipsychotic challenge to test for psychosis
IV lorazepam 2 mg as diagnostic and therapeutic challenge, parallel ECT planning
Intravenous propofol 1 mg/kg for sedation and disimpaction of posturing
Oral bromocriptine 7.5 mg twice daily for presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g empirically while awaiting anti-NMDA receptor antibody

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome after MAOI plus tramadol
stem:
You are the ED registrar called to assess a 38-year-old woman with a 4 year history of refractory depression on phenelzine 60 mg daily who has just been brought in. Her GP prescribed tramadol 100 mg for a severe migraine 4 hours ago, unaware of the MAOI. She took 1 tablet and has rapidly developed agitation, sweating, and shivering. Her husband reports she has been increasingly hot and jittery and she has been vomiting twice.

On examination she is restless and confused with marked diaphoresis. She has rhythmic horizontal eye movements (ocular clonus), hyperreflexia particularly in the lower limbs with sustained ankle clonus, and increased lower limb tone. Pupils are dilated. She is on no other psychotropics and has no infective contacts. She has had no antipsychotic exposure. Phenelzine has been ceased today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 162/98 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Restless, confused; ocular clonus; lower limb hyperreflexia with sustained ankle clonus; pupils dilated; bowel sounds increased; lower limb hypertonia greater than upper limb
data_table.Investigations: CK 1200 U/L (40-200); K 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90); venous gas pH 7.36, lactate 2.8 mmol/L; FBC and coags pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous haloperidol 5 mg plus surface cooling with cold packs only
Intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg as first-line agent for hyperthermia
Cease both agents, give IV benzodiazepines plus cooling plus IV fluids
Intravenous cyproheptadine 32 mg loading dose immediately as primary therapy
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg for presumed TCA-like cardiotoxicity

subtopic_detail: Valproate in women of childbearing potential - switch planning
stem:
A 22-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is reviewed in the psychiatry outpatient clinic. She has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for the past 3 years with full remission. Her past episodes were all manic with psychotic features, with no significant depressive episodes recorded. She has recently become engaged and discloses that she would like to conceive within the next 1-2 years.

She has read about valproate-associated congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental effects and asks how to plan ahead safely. She has never had a trial of lithium or atypical antipsychotic monotherapy. She drinks no alcohol, does not smoke, and her thyroid function and renal function are within normal limits. There is no family history of bipolar disorder treatment failure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic; well groomed; no psychomotor disturbance; insight intact; future-oriented goals appropriate to current life stage
data_table.Investigations: Valproate level 410 micromol/L (350-700); TSH 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); creatinine 65 micromol/L (45-90), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m²; BHCG negative this morning at clinic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in medication planning?

options.text: Continue current dose of valproate with high dose folate 5 mg daily, detailed pre-conception counselling about teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks, and proceed to conception when ready
Cease valproate abruptly now and observe medication free for the next 6 months to confirm stability before any other agent is introduced or pregnancy is planned by the patient
Switch directly to carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily as the primary alternative mood stabiliser with the same efficacy profile and a more favourable pregnancy safety profile than valproate
Switch to olanzapine 10 mg orally nocte as the maintenance agent for mania-predominant bipolar I with planned pregnancy in the next 2 years, with monthly mental state and metabolic monitoring

Switch under specialist supervision to lithium with serum level and mood monitoring, confirm stability for at least 6 months on the new agent before conception, and arrange fetal echocardiography in pregnancy

stem:
A 28-year-old male software developer is reviewed in the general adult psychiatry outpatient clinic with 6 months of persistent inattention, distractibility, restlessness and difficulty completing tasks at work. School reports document similar features from age 7. ASRS-v1.1 screener is 6 of 6 positive. He requests stimulant treatment after researching options online.

His mother had a myocardial infarction at age 55. His father has hypertension on amlodipine. He has no personal history of cardiac symptoms, syncope, palpitations or exercise intolerance. He drinks 4 standard drinks per week and uses no illicit drugs. His weight is 75 kg and BMI 24. There are no features of psychosis or current mood disorder. He has not previously trialled stimulants or atomoxetine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 120/78 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mental state appropriate to interview; affect reactive; no psychomotor disturbance; cardiac auscultation dual heart sounds no murmurs; no signs of anxiety disorder beyond ADHD-attributable restlessness
data_table.Investigations: FBC, electrolytes, thyroid function, liver function within normal limits; urine drug screen negative; no ECG or cardiac investigations performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before initiating treatment?

options.text: Perform 12-lead ECG and obtain a focused personal and family cardiovascular history with examination before commencing stimulant therapy and arrange a 3 month BP and HR review on treatment
Commence methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg orally twice daily immediately and arrange a follow up review in 4 weeks to assess clinical response and tolerability to the stimulant therapy
Refer to cardiology for a stress echocardiogram and 24 hour Holter monitor before any consideration of starting a stimulant medication, due to family history of myocardial infarction in mother at 55

Recommend cognitive behavioural therapy alone without medication for the next 6 months given the family history of cardiovascular disease, then reassess for pharmacotherapy after the behavioural trial
Trial of atomoxetine 40 mg orally daily without further investigation as a non-stimulant first-line agent that avoids any cardiovascular concerns associated with stimulant medications for adult ADHD

subtopic_detail: Borderline PD recurrent self-harm community management
stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a 3-year diagnosis of borderline personality disorder presents to the emergency department for the fourth time this month following superficial cutting of her left forearm. She denies any current suicidal intent. She lives alone in stable accommodation and is engaged with a community case manager and a weekly dialectical behaviour therapy group. Her last admission to hospital was 8 months ago.

On examination she is calm but distressed, asking to be admitted overnight because she does not feel safe at home tonight. The wounds are superficial and have been cleaned and steri-stripped. She has no acute mood or psychotic symptoms. Her case manager is contactable and there is a written safety plan from her DBT therapist in her file. She has no substance intoxication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Calm but distressed; no psychomotor agitation; no thought disorder; denies current suicidal intent or plan; superficial cuts cleaned and dressed; no active substance intoxication
data_table.Investigations: Routine bloods unremarkable; urine drug screen negative; ECG sinus rhythm rate 84; written safety plan from DBT therapist available in file

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition for this patient?

options.text: Voluntary inpatient admission to the acute psychiatric ward for at least 72 hours of observation, milieu support, daily medical review and intensive behavioural and pharmacological intervention monitoring

Discharge home with same-day contact to community case manager, safety plan review, DBT crisis skills coaching call within 24 hours, and a planned follow-up DBT group within 72 hours by current therapy provider

Compulsory admission under the Mental Health Act to a closed ward for 7 days observation given the frequency of recurrent ED presentations with deliberate self-harm despite community supports being in place

Referral to community addictions service for substance use assessment and treatment as the primary intervention rather than ongoing mental health and dialectical behaviour therapy follow up arrangements
Increase quetiapine to 200 mg orally at night as a sleep and behavioural stabilising medication to reduce her impulsivity, with weekly mental health team review of mood and self-harm behaviour

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal in decompensated liver disease - benzodiazepine choice
stem:
A 58-year-old man is admitted to the gastroenterology ward 8 hours ago for management of acute alcohol withdrawal. He drinks approximately 350 g of alcohol per day (35 standard drinks) and has not had a drink for 18 hours. He has known biopsy-proven cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class B) with ascites managed by spironolactone, and is being worked up for liver transplantation.

He is tremulous, diaphoretic, and anxious. He is fully oriented to person, place and time, with no current hallucinations and no seizures. CIWA-Ar score is 22. He has had thiamine 300 mg intravenously already. There is no acute infection. He has not yet had any benzodiazepine. He has had no withdrawal seizures in the past.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 110/min, BP 158/95 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Tremulous and diaphoretic; oriented to person/place/time; no hallucinations; no asterixis; abdomen distended with mild ascites; no encephalopathy
data_table.Investigations: INR 1.8 (0.9-1.2), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), bilirubin 45 micromol/L (<20), ALT 80 U/L (<40), platelets 90 x10⁹/L (150-400); ammonia 60 micromol/L (<35); ethanol level negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate benzodiazepine regimen?

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally on a symptom triggered regimen every 1 to 2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar below 8 with target dose ceiling of 80 mg in 24 hours and clinical review thereafter
Lorazepam 1 mg orally on a regular regimen with continuous intravenous midazolam infusion as background sedation to control acute autonomic withdrawal symptoms over the first 24 hours
Oxazepam 15 to 30 mg orally on a symptom triggered regimen every 1 to 2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar below 8 with clinical reassessment and downward titration once acute autonomic symptoms settle
Chlordiazepoxide 50 mg orally every 6 hours on a fixed schedule for 5 days followed by tapering over the next 3 days regardless of clinical course of withdrawal during the first 48 hours
Phenobarbital 30 mg orally three times daily as a primary first line agent and arrange referral to addiction medicine for ongoing outpatient relapse prevention follow up after discharge

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome detection on day 2 of refeed
stem:
A 17-year-old girl has been admitted to the adolescent medicine ward with severe anorexia nervosa. Her BMI is 13.2 kg/m² with 28% weight loss over the past 6 months. She has been eating minimally for the past 4 months. Initial admission bloods: K 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Mg 0.65 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), PO4 0.7 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), albumin 30 g/L (35-50). ECG shows QTc 460 ms. Refeeding was commenced 36 hours ago at 1200 kcal/day with thiamine 300 mg IV and oral multivitamin supplementation.

This morning's repeat bloods (day 2 of refeeding) show: K 2.7, Mg 0.55, PO4 0.4. Calcium 2.20 mmol/L (2.10-2.55) corrected. She is asymptomatic with no peripheral oedema, no Chvostek or Trousseau sign, normal cardiac auscultation, and ambulating well. Vital signs are unchanged from admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56/min, BP 95/60 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Cachectic; alert, oriented; no peripheral oedema; Chvostek and Trousseau negative; normal cardiac auscultation; weight 36 kg (admission 36 kg)
data_table.Investigations: Day 2 K 2.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Mg 0.55 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), PO4 0.4 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), corrected Ca 2.20 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), albumin 28 g/L (35-50); ECG QTc 470 ms; bedside glucose 4.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adjustment to her refeeding plan?

options.text: Continue the current 1200 kcal/day caloric target as planned and supplement potassium, phosphate and magnesium orally only, with serial bloods every 24 hours for the next 4 days while on the ward
Increase caloric intake to 1800 kcal/day to better restore body weight quickly and add a multivitamin tablet daily, with daily bloods monitored on the adolescent medicine ward for the first week
Stop refeeding entirely for the next 48 hours and reassess electrolytes and weight before recommencing nutritional support to allow the metabolic disturbance to fully correct prior to nutrition

Reduce caloric intake to maintenance level, replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium intravenously with thiamine 300 mg IV continued, and monitor electrolytes 6 hourly with continuous cardiac monitoring
Transfer the patient to intensive care now and commence total parenteral nutrition with insulin to manage glucose homeostasis during refeeding and intubate for airway protection given her cachexia

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis with infant-directed command hallucinations
stem:
A 31-year-old G1P1 woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband on day 6 postpartum because she is making no sense and has not slept for 3 days. She believes the baby is dead inside and that she must send him back. She has had a previous diagnosis of bipolar I disorder with manic-only episodes, well controlled on lithium 750 mg nocte which she ceased 6 months prior to conception under specialist advice.

The baby is currently being cared for by the patient's mother at home and is well. The patient is currently exclusively breastfeeding. On mental state examination she is agitated with disorganised speech, with auditory hallucinations telling her to send the baby back, and persecutory delusions about hospital staff. There are no focal neurological signs and no signs of sepsis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 105/min, BP 130/82 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Agitated, disorganised, command auditory hallucinations directed at infant; persecutory delusions; no focal neurology; reflexes symmetric; no neck stiffness; perineum healing well
data_table.Investigations: FBC, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, glucose, LFTs within normal limits; TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); urine drug screen negative; B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg orally now and discharge home with husband supervision, with outpatient psychiatry review within 24 hours and community mental health team contact within the working day
Recommence sertraline 50 mg orally daily as postpartum depression treatment with weekly community mental health team review for ongoing assessment and supportive management in the home environment

Same-day electroconvulsive therapy in the emergency department with brief consent process before any transfer to inpatient psychiatric care or mother baby unit elsewhere in the regional health network

Compulsory admission to a general medical ward for overnight observation, pending formal psychiatry review in the morning, with husband requested to remain at bedside throughout for safety and support
Involuntary admission to a Mother-Baby Unit with olanzapine, lithium reintroduction with breastfeeding cessation, and ECT consideration if response is inadequate within 48 to 72 hours of admission

stem:
A 54-year-old man with a 20-year history of bipolar I disorder is brought to a metropolitan emergency department by his wife. He has been increasingly tremulous and unsteady on his feet over the past 4 days. He vomited twice this morning before presentation. He is normally maintained on lithium carbonate 800 mg nightly, with the last serum lithium level at 0.7 mmol/L two months ago. His wife notes that he began ramipril 5 mg daily 3 weeks ago for newly diagnosed hypertension by his GP.

On examination he is awake but drowsy and has coarse hand tremor and ataxia on standing. He is oriented to person but not place or date. Speech is dysarthric. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus. The abdomen is soft, mucous membranes dry. His regular lithium dose was taken this morning at home. A bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 460 ms; no T wave changes. Vital signs are stable. The toxicology service has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, coarse hand tremor, dysarthria, brisk reflexes with sustained ankle clonus, ataxia on standing; mucous membranes dry; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 2.4 mmol/L (0.4-1.0), sodium 144 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 165 micromol/L (baseline 78); TSH within normal limits; bicarbonate 22 mmol/L; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 460 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Hold the next dose of lithium and recheck serum lithium level in 12 hours while continuing oral fluids and rest at home with the wife monitoring symptoms
Stop lithium and ramipril, give intravenous 0.9% saline at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance and refer urgently to nephrology for consideration of haemodialysis
Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally now as a single dose to reduce lithium absorption and to limit further increases in serum lithium concentration
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg now and aim to alkalinise the urine to a pH greater than 7.5 to increase the renal elimination of lithium
Substitute oral lithium with intravenous sodium valproate loading dose 20 mg/kg to maintain mood stabilisation throughout the management of his lithium toxicity

stem:
A 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine for 18 days, currently titrated to 200 mg nightly. He attends his community mental health clinic for routine review and reports 4 days of intermittent fevers up to 38.4 °C, fatigue, and one episode of palpitations the night before. He denies cough, dysuria, or rash. His neutrophil count remains within range on weekly FBC monitoring.

On examination he appears tired but alert. He has resting tachycardia at 116/min and warm peripheries. Heart sounds are dual, no murmurs are audible. Chest is clear. There is no calf tenderness or rash. The clinic nurse has obtained the standard week-2 clozapine screening bloods earlier today. He is otherwise compliant with his medication and lives with his mother who reports no concerning behaviours. He has had no recent overseas travel.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 124/74 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Tachycardic regular rhythm, no murmurs, no pericardial rub, no lower limb oedema; clear chest; no rash; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 3.6 x10^9/L (1.5-7.5); CRP 86 mg/L (<5); troponin I 65 ng/L (<14); ALT within normal limits; bedside ECG sinus tachycardia, no ST changes, no T wave inversion; viral swab not yet sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold the next clozapine dose, refer urgently to the emergency department for transthoracic echocardiography and same-day cardiology review including repeat troponin
Continue clozapine at the same dose, start oral paracetamol for the fever and recheck inflammatory markers and troponin in 5 days at the next routine clinic appointment
Switch from clozapine to olanzapine immediately at an equivalent dose and arrange a routine follow up appointment with his community psychiatrist within 2 weeks
Repeat the full blood count and inflammatory markers urgently and only refer to the emergency department if the absolute neutrophil count drops below 1.5 x10^9/L this morning
Withhold clozapine and commence oral roxithromycin 300 mg daily for 7 days empirically for atypical respiratory infection given the fevers, tachycardia and elevated CRP

subtopic_detail: SSRI choice in early pregnancy with prior remission
stem:
A 31-year-old G2P1 woman attends her GP at 7 weeks gestation. She has been in remission from a moderate major depressive episode for the past 18 months on paroxetine 20 mg daily. Her first child is now 3 years old; she had antenatal anxiety but no significant relapse during that previous pregnancy on the same medication. She and her partner planned this pregnancy and were aware that paroxetine has a different safety profile in pregnancy.

She is currently euthymic with stable mood, sleep, and appetite. She has no suicidal ideation. She had one mild relapse during a previous attempt to discontinue paroxetine 2 years ago. Her medical history is otherwise unremarkable and she is on no other medications. Folate 5 mg daily was started by her GP at preconception counselling. The GP has asked your community perinatal mental health service for an opinion on the medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Euthymic affect, full range; no psychomotor change; no psychotic features; no thoughts of self-harm; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: FBC, electrolytes, thyroid function, vitamin D within normal limits; bhCG positive (date-concordant); fetal ultrasound at 6 weeks confirmed single intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her antidepressant management?

options.text: Cease paroxetine immediately and review her in 4 weeks for symptomatic relapse and consider non-pharmacological therapy if symptoms recur during her pregnancy
Refer to perinatal psychiatry for an inpatient assessment and consideration of electroconvulsive therapy because she has a relapsing major depressive episode in pregnancy
Continue paroxetine 20 mg daily as her current effective treatment given the risks of relapse outweigh any small concerns regarding paroxetine in pregnancy outcomes
Switch paroxetine to mirtazapine 15 mg nightly with reassessment in 4 weeks given mirtazapine has a better established safety profile in pregnancy than the SSRI class
Cross-taper from paroxetine to sertraline 50 mg daily over 2 weeks and continue throughout pregnancy and lactation given her history of relapse on discontinuation

stem:
A 45-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is admitted to a general medical ward after her family found her standing in the kitchen at home, not moving and not responding for 4 hours. She had stopped eating and drinking 36 hours earlier. Her usual medications are lithium and quetiapine. Her last manic episode was 3 years ago; she has had two previous similar episodes which the family describes as periods of complete withdrawal. There is no recent fever, illness, or drug use.

On arrival she is mute, with a fixed waxy posture of her arms held above the head when placed by the examiner, which she maintains for over 5 minutes. She does not respond to verbal command but tracks the examiner with her eyes. She has rigidity without tremor. Bedside fluids and an indwelling urinary catheter have been placed. Her recent lithium level was therapeutic. Bloods are unremarkable. CT head shows no acute findings. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score is 16.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility (catalepsy), arms maintained above head over 5 minutes; tracking with eyes; rigidity without tremor; no fever, no clonus, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea and creatinine within normal limits; CK 168 U/L; lithium level 0.8 mmol/L; venous blood gas pH 7.40; CT head no acute findings; bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale 16

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg in addition to her usual psychiatric medications targeting the rigidity component present on her clinical examination today
Refer urgently for unilateral right-sided electroconvulsive therapy under general anaesthesia at the next available list before any pharmacological intervention is trialled first
Increase her quetiapine to 600 mg daily for better antipsychotic cover and continue supportive care with intravenous fluids and nasogastric feeding for nutrition
Administer lorazepam 2 mg intravenously as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge and reassess catatonic features and Bush-Francis score within 30 to 60 minutes
Hold lithium and quetiapine for 24 hours and reassess catatonic features tomorrow morning with the consultant psychiatry team before any further therapeutic intervention

subtopic_detail: Duration of therapy after a successful quit
stem: A 50-year-old man finishes twelve weeks of varenicline today and has not smoked for eleven weeks. He describes daily cravings when he drinks coffee with colleagues and fears relapsing once the course ends.

data_table.Course: Varenicline 1 mg twice daily, twelve weeks completed
data_table.Now: Abstinent 11 weeks; cravings most days; treatment well tolerated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue varenicline a further twelve weeks with behavioural support
Stop varenicline today and supply nicotine lozenges for residual cravings
Stop varenicline and taper the dose over the coming two weeks
Stop varenicline and start bupropion for a further twelve weeks
Stop varenicline and review him only if he starts smoking again

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD pharmacotherapy choice in cocaine history
stem:
A 28-year-old man self-refers to a private psychiatry practice for assessment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He describes lifelong distractibility, difficulty completing tasks, hyperactivity, and emotional dysregulation. Symptoms started before age 12 and have impaired schooling, employment, and relationships. A teacher-completed Vanderbilt scale from his year 4 school report flags 7 of 9 inattentive items.

He is currently a software developer but has been performance managed twice in the last 12 months. He drinks 4 standard drinks weekly. He used cocaine recreationally for 4 years and stopped 18 months ago after a near-fatal cardiac arrhythmia event in a nightclub. He has no current substance use. He has no other psychiatric history. ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms and otherwise normal. Echocardiogram (recent) was normal. He is asking specifically about medication options.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mental state examination - mood euthymic, attention impaired during interview, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: FBC, electrolytes, LFTs, thyroid within normal limits; urine drug screen negative; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms; echocardiogram normal LV function; ASRS-v1.1 score 6 of 6 positive screening items

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best initial pharmacotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Methylphenidate immediate-release 5 mg twice daily titrated weekly as first-line stimulant therapy given his clear positive screening and lifelong impairment
Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily titrated weekly as a long-acting prodrug stimulant with smoother pharmacokinetics and lower diversion potential than other stimulants
Guanfacine extended-release 1 mg daily titrated weekly to 4 mg daily as a non-stimulant alpha-2 agonist given his history of stimulant-induced cardiac arrhythmia event
Bupropion sustained-release 150 mg daily for 3 days then 150 mg twice daily for ADHD as an off-label noradrenergic-dopaminergic option given his stimulant contraindication
