Atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrated to 80 mg after 1 week as a non-stimulant first-line agent given his history of stimulant-induced cardiac arrhythmia and current ADHD diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features
stem:
A 30-year-old woman is reviewed in a community psychiatry clinic with an established treating psychiatrist. She has had three episodes of significant mood disturbance over the last 8 years: two manic-like episodes with grandiose delusions and one major depressive episode with mood-congruent persecutory delusions. Between the second manic episode and the major depressive episode 18 months later, she had a continuous 12-week period of clear-cut auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions without prominent mood symptoms; her mood was reported as euthymic by her partner and family throughout that interval.

She has been on olanzapine 15 mg nightly during episodes and has had remission of psychosis after each episode. She has not used substances. Family history includes a maternal aunt with schizophrenia and a paternal grandfather with bipolar I disorder. Current mental state is euthymic with no psychotic features. The clinic is considering revising her diagnostic formulation. Cognition is intact, no neurological signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mental state - euthymic, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation; cognition intact on MMSE 30 of 30
data_table.Investigations: Bloods - FBC, electrolytes, LFTs, TSH, vitamin B12 within normal limits; urine drug screen negative; CT brain (historical, 4 years ago) normal; MRI brain (historical, 18 months ago) normal

lead_in: Based on the longitudinal course described, what is the most likely DSM-5-TR diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features in the most recent depressive episode and grandiose features in the prior manic episodes during the illness history

Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type with the lifetime presence of a major mood episode concurrent with criterion A schizophrenia symptoms and 2 or more weeks of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood symptoms
Schizophrenia with comorbid recurrent major depressive disorder and manic features attributable to substance use because the diagnosis of psychosis is supported by clear hallucinations
Schizophreniform disorder with affective features and a brief duration of mood symptoms within the context of a primary psychotic illness over the last 8 years of her psychiatric history
Delusional disorder mixed type with secondary mood symptoms occurring intermittently and the longitudinal course best characterised by persistent encapsulated non-bizarre delusions

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome with linezolid and SSRI
stem:
A 38-year-old man with chronic recurrent diabetic foot osteomyelitis is admitted to a metropolitan hospital for intravenous antibiotic therapy. He has been taking sertraline 100 mg daily for 6 years for major depressive disorder; mood is in remission. The infectious diseases team commenced intravenous linezolid 36 hours ago for MRSA cover after culture results returned. He was previously stable on oral sertraline through the admission process.

This morning he becomes agitated, confused, and hyperthermic. Nursing staff document inducible clonus in both lower limbs, hyperreflexia worse in the lower limbs than upper, mydriasis, diaphoresis, and a tremor. Sodium and bicarbonate are normal. There is no neck stiffness, no rash, no photophobia. He has had no sympathomimetic medications. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria are met. The medical team are calling for advice on management.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 168/96 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Agitated and confused, lower-limb-dominant hyperreflexia and inducible clonus, mydriasis, diaphoresis, fine tremor; no neck stiffness; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea and creatinine within normal limits; CK 1820 U/L; venous blood gas pH 7.34, lactate 3.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management priority alongside ICU referral and active cooling?

options.text: Administer intravenous bromocriptine 2.5 mg three times daily as a dopaminergic rescue for the hyperthermic syndrome and continue the linezolid and sertraline at full dose throughout
Commence intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg as muscle relaxation for the hyperthermia and rigidity and continue both linezolid and sertraline because the infection requires ongoing treatment
Switch linezolid to vancomycin and continue sertraline because vancomycin does not interact with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and infection treatment must continue
Stop linezolid and sertraline, give intravenous benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, and consider cyproheptadine 12 mg orally if features persist after first-line measures
Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg slow injection for the agitation and confusion and continue current medications while waiting for the toxicology consultant review

stem:
A 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium 750 mg at night for the past 18 months following hospitalisation for a manic episode. She is reviewed in the community mental health clinic.

She has had no mood episodes, no medication side effects, and has been working full time. Her last serum lithium level was 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6 to 0.8 for maintenance) six months ago. Her last full set of monitoring bloods was at the time of initiation 18 months ago, which she completed without prompting. She brings printed copies of those baseline results, all of which were within normal limits including TSH, calcium, creatinine, and full blood count.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: no fine tremor, no goitre, euthymic mood, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: last lithium level 0.7 mmol/L six months ago; no monitoring bloods done since initiation 18 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring schedule?

options.text: Lithium level annually with TSH, creatinine and calcium only if symptomatic
Lithium level monthly and TSH plus creatinine 3-monthly indefinitely
Lithium level only when dose changes or symptoms suggest toxicity or relapse
Lithium level 6-monthly with full blood count alone every 12 months
Lithium level 6-monthly; TSH and creatinine 6-monthly; calcium and FBC 12-monthly

stem:
A 24-year-old man with first-episode psychosis was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nightly two months ago after presenting to the early psychosis intervention service. He has responded well: persecutory delusions have resolved and he is sleeping consistently. He has no past medical history, does not smoke, and drinks alcohol once or twice a month.

Baseline assessment at the time of starting olanzapine included weight 78 kg, BMI 24, BP 122 by 78 mmHg, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L (less than 5.5), LDL 2.4 mmol/L, HDL 1.3 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.0 mmol/L, and a normal ECG. He attends a routine community follow-up appointment.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: no extrapyramidal signs, no postural drop
data_table.Investigations: baseline weight 78 kg BMI 24, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, LDL 2.4, HDL 1.3, triglycerides 1.0, ECG normal

lead_in: When is the next set of antipsychotic-related metabolic monitoring bloods due?

options.text: At 12 weeks from initiation (around 4 weeks from now), then annually if stable
At 6 weeks from initiation, then 12 weeks, then annually if stable on therapy
At 6 months from initiation, then annually if metabolic measures remain stable
At 12 months from initiation if asymptomatic, then yearly thereafter on therapy
Only if weight gain, hypertension, or new symptoms develop on therapy

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of acute behavioural disturbance
stem:
A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics under a section of the Mental Health Act after threatening neighbours with a baseball bat. He has a documented history of schizophrenia and methamphetamine use. He has not taken any prescribed medications for the past two weeks.

In the resuscitation cubicle he is shouting, pacing, and intermittently striking the walls. Verbal de-escalation by experienced mental health nurses for 20 minutes has failed. Security staff are present. Pulse is 110, blood pressure 138 by 84 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius. He weighs approximately 80 kg. He is now physically restrained. There is no history of cardiac disease, no QT-prolonging medications, and no opioid use.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 138/84, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: agitated, mydriasis, no diaphoresis, no clonus, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: weight approximately 80 kg; no ECG yet; no recent QT-prolonging medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally with continued verbal de-escalation effort
Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg with separated benzodiazepine if needed later
Combined IM haloperidol 10 mg plus IM lorazepam 2 mg given simultaneously now
Oral quetiapine 300 mg with continued seclusion until adequate sedation occurs
Continue physical restraint and seclusion only without pharmacological intervention

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS prolongation
stem:
A 42-year-old woman with major depressive disorder is brought to the emergency department by her partner approximately two hours after ingesting an unknown quantity of her amitriptyline 50 mg tablets in a deliberate self-poisoning event. The original 100-tablet bottle is now empty.

On arrival she is drowsy with GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5), pulse 128, blood pressure 92 by 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius. Pupils are 6 mm bilaterally and reactive. She has dry mucous membranes and absent bowel sounds. The 12-lead ECG demonstrates sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 132 ms and a terminal R wave of 4 mm in lead aVR. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.30, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32). Potassium is 3.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). Paracetamol level is undetectable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 92/58, RR 14, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E3V3M5), dry mucous membranes, absent bowel sounds, pupils 6 mm reactive
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, QRS 132 ms, terminal R wave aVR 4 mm; pH 7.30, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32), K 3.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); paracetamol undetectable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g orally with intravenous fluids and observation only
Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg followed by intravenous fluid resuscitation
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, then titrate to pH 7.5
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus over 15 minutes for arrhythmia prevention
Intravenous lidocaine infusion at 1 to 4 mg/min for ventricular arrhythmia prevention

subtopic_detail: Valproate use in women of childbearing potential
stem:
A 27-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for two years. Prior to valproate she had three manic episodes requiring hospitalisation, two of which were precipitated by lithium discontinuation due to renal concerns at the time (creatinine has since normalised). Her current valproate level is 500 micromol/L (350-700) and her last manic episode was three years ago.

She attends her psychiatry follow-up to share that she and her partner are planning to conceive within the next 6 to 12 months. She has been using a contraceptive intrauterine device since starting valproate. There is no relevant family history, no medical comorbidity, and she takes no other medications.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: euthymic, no extrapyramidal signs, no fine tremor
data_table.Investigations: valproate level 500 micromol/L (350-700); LFTs, FBC, creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication-management plan?

options.text: Continue valproate with high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily during planning and pregnancy
Continue valproate until pregnancy confirmed, then cease and switch to lamotrigine
Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily during planning to minimise teratogenicity risk overall
Cross-titrate from valproate to lithium with cardiology echo screen and pre-conception planning
Stop valproate immediately and commence high-dose olanzapine 20 mg nightly indefinitely

subtopic_detail: Lithium continuation in pregnancy for bipolar I
stem:
A 31-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is referred to the perinatal mental health clinic at 6 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She has been stable on lithium 900 mg nightly for four years after a severe manic episode that required involuntary admission. She has had two further close calls with mood escalation, both of which resolved promptly when her lithium dose was adjusted upward.

She reports unplanned but very welcomed pregnancy and is anxious about her medication. Her current lithium level is 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6 to 0.8). She has booked with a community midwife and has a supportive partner and family. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago. She has no other medications and the pregnancy ultrasound at 6 weeks confirmed a viable intrauterine pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: euthymic mood, no fine tremor, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8); creatinine and TSH within normal limits; viable 6-wk IUP on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her lithium during pregnancy?

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and substitute olanzapine 10 mg nightly throughout pregnancy
Continue lithium at lowest effective dose, divide doses, and arrange fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks
Reduce lithium dose by 50 percent immediately to mitigate first-trimester teratogenic risk
Cross-titrate lithium to lamotrigine over 4 weeks during the first trimester
Continue lithium unchanged with no additional monitoring beyond routine antenatal care

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome from linezolid plus SSRI
stem:
A 58-year-old woman is admitted with a 36-hour history of confusion, sweating, and shaking limbs. She has a longstanding history of major depressive disorder and has been on escitalopram 20 mg daily for two years. Eight days ago she was started on linezolid 600 mg twice daily for a multi-drug-resistant skin and soft tissue infection in the orthopaedic ward.

On examination she is agitated and confused, with pulse 124, blood pressure 170 by 96 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius. There is sustained ankle clonus bilaterally, generalised hyperreflexia, ocular clonus, and intermittent tremor. Pupils are 6 mm bilaterally. Muscle tone is increased but not lead-pipe rigid. Creatine kinase is 480 U/L (less than 200). White cell count 11.0 x10^9/L (4-11) and CRP 18 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 170/96, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: agitated, sustained ankle clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia, ocular clonus, mydriasis, increased tone without lead-pipe rigidity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combination of immediate management actions?

options.text: Continue escitalopram and linezolid, IV cefazolin and dantrolene for presumed NMS
Cease escitalopram and linezolid, IV benzodiazepines, active cooling, oral cyproheptadine 12 mg
Cease escitalopram only, continue linezolid, IV haloperidol 5 mg for agitation control
Cease linezolid only, continue escitalopram, paracetamol and IV fluids for fever control
Cease both drugs, give IV bromocriptine 2.5 mg eight hourly and supportive care only

subtopic_detail: Refractory delirium tremens despite high-dose diazepam
stem:
A 54-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence is admitted with severe alcohol withdrawal 48 hours after his last drink. He is on a symptom-triggered diazepam regimen using the CIWA-Ar scale, has received 180 mg of diazepam orally over the past 8 hours, and additional 20 mg IV doses in the past hour.

He remains agitated with visual hallucinations of insects on the walls, tremor, and disorientation to place and time. Vital signs are pulse 138, blood pressure 172 by 102 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. There is no rigidity. He has received pabrinex (high-potency parenteral B and C vitamins). Magnesium and phosphate were replaced 6 hours ago and remain within normal limits. His CIWA-Ar score is 28 (severe). Liver function shows AST 88 U/L (less than 40), ALT 55 U/L (less than 40), bilirubin 24 micromol/L, INR 1.3.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 172/102, RR 24, SpO2 95% room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: tremor, visual hallucinations of insects, disoriented to place and time, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: CIWA-Ar 28 (severe); AST 88, ALT 55, bilirubin 24, INR 1.3; magnesium and phosphate within normal limits; cumulative diazepam 200 mg in 8 h

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: IV haloperidol 5 mg with paracetamol 1 g for symptomatic agitation and fever
IV dexmedetomidine infusion 0.4 microgram/kg/h with continued benzodiazepine infusion
Oral baclofen 10 mg three times daily and continue current diazepam protocol
Switch to oxazepam 60 mg every 2 hours and continue symptom-triggered scoring intervals
IV phenobarbital 130 to 260 mg loading dose, then titrated to symptom control

stem:
A 28-year-old man with first-episode psychosis was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nightly six weeks ago by the early psychosis team. His psychotic symptoms have settled, his sleep has improved, and he is back at his apprenticeship. He has gained 3 kg since starting and is generally well. He attends your community mental health clinic for routine review.

Baseline bloods taken when olanzapine was started showed fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4), HbA1c 5.2%, total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, LDL 2.4 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.0 mmol/L. ECG showed a QTc of 410 ms. Weight at baseline was 78 kg; today 81 kg. There is no personal or family history of diabetes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: BMI 27 kg/m^2; no signs of EPS, akathisia, or tardive dyskinesia
data_table.Investigations: ongoing weekly weight checks since commencement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next monitoring schedule?

options.text: Recheck metabolic bloods only if he gains more than 7% of his baseline weight
Repeat fasting glucose, lipids, and weight at 12 weeks then yearly thereafter
Switch to quetiapine to reduce metabolic risk and recheck at one year
Add metformin 500 mg twice daily prophylactically to prevent metabolic syndrome
Repeat the ECG every 3 months indefinitely while he remains on olanzapine

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia stable on aripiprazole attends your community mental health clinic. She has smoked 25 cigarettes per day since age 18 and wants to quit because of new chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She has tried nicotine patches twice in the past with limited success.

Her mental state is stable. She has no current depressive features, no suicidal thoughts, and no recent psychotic relapse. She has no past history of seizures or anorexia. She has no significant cardiovascular history. She is keen on a more aggressive pharmacological approach this time, supported by her case manager. She has no contraindications to systemic medication on review of her current chart.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: no nicotine staining of fingers visible (she wears gloves), no oral mucosal lesions
data_table.Investigations: spirometry confirms COPD; FEV1 65% predicted; FBC, UEC, LFT within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion SR 150 mg daily increasing to 150 mg twice daily after a week
Varenicline 1 mg twice daily after one-week escalation, quit date in week 2
Combination patch plus oral nicotine replacement therapy with behavioural support
Off-label nortriptyline 75 mg nightly for smoking cessation support
Clonidine 75 micrograms twice daily titrated to symptoms of nicotine withdrawal

stem:
A 23-year-old woman is referred to your community mental health team following a third presentation in 12 weeks for superficial wrist lacerations after arguments with her partner. She describes intense rage, chronic emptiness, and frantic efforts to avoid being left when relationships strain. She has had three boyfriends and two best friends in two years.

Her mood swings throughout each day between euphoric and tearful. There are no fixed delusions, no command hallucinations, no manic episodes lasting beyond an afternoon, and no full depressive episodes. She has tried two SSRIs over 18 months with limited benefit. She has no substance dependence currently. The team formulation lands on borderline personality disorder by DSM-5-TR criteria.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: mental state: dysphoric, intermittently tearful, reactive affect, no psychosis, no current suicidal intent though chronic suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: no acute medical issues

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Switch the SSRI to venlafaxine extended release as an alternative antidepressant trial
Commence olanzapine 5 mg nightly to stabilise mood and behaviour
Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for mood stabilisation
Plan a brief inpatient admission to contain the behaviour after each episode
Refer for a structured psychological therapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a known diagnosis of bipolar I disorder is brought to the emergency department by her family for being mute, immobile in unusual postures, and not eating or drinking for 36 hours. Her mother says she stopped responding two days ago after stopping her lithium and quetiapine three weeks ago to start a master's degree.

On examination she stares ahead, follows commands occasionally, holds her arm wherever you place it for over 30 seconds, and grimaces. There are no focal neurological signs. She is afebrile. Family report no recent infection, no head injury, no street drug use, and no withdrawal symptoms. There is no rigidity, no autonomic instability, and no fever to suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: stupor, mutism, waxy flexibility, posturing, grimacing; no rigidity, no clonus, no fever
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, CK 220 U/L (40 to 240), TSH 1.6 mIU/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L; CT head non-contrast normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order an immediate lumbar puncture to exclude autoimmune encephalitis
Commence haloperidol 5 mg IM now to treat the underlying psychosis
Restart lithium at the prior maintenance dose to reverse the mood episode driver
Trial IM or IV lorazepam 1 to 2 mg with reassessment of catatonia scale at 30 minutes
Refer for urgent ECT before any pharmacological intervention is given

stem:
A 38-year-old man with major depressive disorder is brought to the emergency department by his housemate with restlessness, sweating, and tremor that began six hours ago. His housemate says he ran out of sertraline two weeks ago and was started on phenelzine three days ago by his private psychiatrist after multiple SSRI failures. He took his usual dose this morning then took two of his housemate's tramadol 50 mg tablets for a sore back.

On arrival he is agitated, has spontaneous clonus in both legs (sustained for several seconds), brisk deep tendon reflexes, ocular clonus, and diaphoresis. There is no muscle rigidity. His pupils are dilated.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 134 /min, blood pressure 168/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: agitated, spontaneous lower limb clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia (4+) more pronounced in lower limbs, dilated pupils, diaphoresis, no lead-pipe rigidity
data_table.Investigations: CK 380 U/L (40 to 240); UEC normal; ABG within normal limits; ECG sinus tachycardia QTc 430 ms; venous lactate 2.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome from MAOI plus tramadol with incomplete SSRI washout
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome with autonomic instability and rigidity
Anticholinergic toxidrome from tramadol's noradrenergic and serotonergic effects
Thyroid storm precipitated by recent infection and tramadol use
Sympathomimetic toxidrome from concurrent stimulant intoxication

stem:
A 64-year-old man with bipolar I disorder on lithium for 15 years presents to the emergency department brought by his daughter with confusion, slurred speech, and tremor that has worsened over a week. She mentions he had a chest infection 10 days ago and was started on an unknown medication by a locum GP. He has remained on his lithium 750 mg twice daily.

On arrival he is drowsy and disoriented to time. He has coarse tremor in both hands, gait ataxia when assisted up, and brisk deep tendon reflexes. There is no fever and no focal neurology. His past medical history includes hypertension on perindopril and chronic kidney disease stage 3.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 64 /min, blood pressure 152/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: drowsy, dysarthric, coarse bilateral hand tremor, gait ataxia, brisk reflexes
data_table.Investigations: lithium level 3.4 mmol/L (0.4 to 1.0); creatinine 180 micromol/L (45 to 90, baseline 110); sodium 138 mmol/L; potassium 4.2 mmol/L; ECG: sinus bradycardia with flattened T waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via a nasogastric tube now
IV 0.9% sodium chloride at 200 mL/hr alone and recheck the level in 6 hours
Arrange urgent haemodialysis after IV 0.9% sodium chloride is commenced
Withhold lithium and recheck levels in 24 hours without other intervention
Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate to lower the lithium level

stem:
A 29-year-old engineer presents to your practice asking about adult ADHD assessment. He describes lifelong difficulty starting and finishing tasks, frequent forgetfulness, fidgeting through meetings, and a pattern of late submissions throughout university and at work. School reports from age 8 noted disorganisation and inattention; he completed his degree but struggled. He has no history of mood or psychotic disorder, no substance dependence, no head injury, and no medical illness on review.

His cardiovascular history is unremarkable. His resting pulse is 72 /min and BP 122/78 mmHg. He has no personal or family history of structural heart disease, sudden death under 40, or unexplained syncope. His full mental state and neurological examination today are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: no abnormal findings; cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: thyroid function, FBC, UEC all within normal limits; ECG sinus rhythm rate 72 with no abnormalities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure adult-onset ADHD is rare and offer CBT for organisation skills only
Trial methylphenidate 10 mg twice daily in the practice and review in 2 weeks
Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily and titrate up to 80 mg over 2 weeks
Refer for neuropsychological testing as the diagnostic gold standard
Refer to a psychiatrist or paediatrician with stimulant authority for diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate in women of childbearing age
stem:
A 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder attends your psychiatry outpatient clinic for review. She has been stable on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years with no relapses. She tells you that she and her partner are planning a pregnancy in the next 6 months. She is not currently using contraception.

She has a documented history of three manic episodes prior to commencing valproate, the last with a brief admission under the Mental Health Act for risk of harm to others. She has not had a depressive episode since valproate initiation. She has no comorbid medical conditions. She has not previously trialled lithium or lamotrigine.

data_table.Examination: well-groomed, euthymic mood, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, normal cognition, BMI 24, no neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: current valproate level 78 micromol/L (therapeutic 350-700 not routinely targeted), full blood count and liver function within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative today, beta-hCG not done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue valproate and add high-dose folate 5 mg daily, reviewing in pregnancy if it occurs in the next 6 months
Continue valproate at current dose and provide written advice on neural tube defect risk plus high-dose folate
Cease valproate over 4 weeks and commence lithium 400 mg nocte plus Pregnancy Prevention Program until conception planned
Switch valproate directly to lamotrigine 25 mg daily with stepwise titration as the primary maintenance choice
Cease valproate immediately and trial olanzapine 10 mg nocte as monotherapy maintenance instead of mood stabilisers

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose - sodium bicarbonate threshold
stem:
A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 90 minutes after ingesting an unknown quantity of his amitriptyline tablets in a suicide attempt. He has a history of treatment-resistant depression and recurrent self-harm. He is drowsy, with intermittent confusion. The ambulance team note he had two brief generalised seizures on the way in that resolved without treatment.

In the resus bay the ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 132 /min with a QRS width of 130 milliseconds and a terminal R wave in aVR of 4 mm. The blood pressure is 92/56 mmHg. He is alert to voice and protecting his airway for now. Capillary blood glucose is 5.4 mmol/L. The poisons information service has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: drowsy but rousable to voice, GCS 13, dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils, reduced bowel sounds, urinary retention on bladder scan, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia QRS 130 ms terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm, venous blood gas pH 7.32 pCO2 36 mmHg lactate 2.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous lidocaine 1 mg/kg as a bolus for the wide-complex tachycardia and ongoing sodium channel blockade
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes for the QRS widening and the risk of ventricular arrhythmia
Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube as primary gastrointestinal decontamination for the tricyclic ingestion
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg over 5 minutes targeting pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS below 100 ms
Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg as a bolus to reverse the central nervous system depression and protect the airway

stem:
A 24-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is on day 19 of a clozapine titration on the inpatient ward. He is currently on clozapine 200 mg daily and tolerating it. On routine surveillance bloods today (week 3 of the AU clozapine monitoring protocol) his troponin I has risen from less than 5 ng/L two days ago to 86 ng/L (less than 14). He reports mild chest tightness for the last day, which he attributed to anxiety.

His CRP is 38 mg/L (under 5), creatine kinase is 240 U/L (45-250), and ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 112 /min with no acute changes. He has had no fever. His haematology and metabolic surveillance bloods are otherwise unremarkable. The clozapine clinic registrar is contactable; the next clozapine dose is due in 4 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 112 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert and oriented, mild chest tightness on direct questioning, no peripheral oedema, no S3 or murmur, lungs clear, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: troponin I 86 ng/L (under 14), CRP 38 mg/L (under 5), creatine kinase 240 U/L (45-250), ECG sinus tachycardia 112 /min no acute changes, NT-proBNP not yet returned

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a routine outpatient stress echocardiogram in 2 weeks and continue current clozapine therapy
Continue clozapine at the same dose and repeat troponin and CRP in 48 hours to confirm a sustained rise
Increase the clozapine dose to 250 mg to overcome the dose-related side effects with clinical review in 1 week
Commence empirical intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days for autoimmune-mediated myocarditis
Withhold the next clozapine dose, arrange urgent echocardiogram and cardiology review for suspected clozapine-induced myocarditis

stem:
A 17-year-old girl is brought to the paediatric emergency department by her general practitioner with concerns about anorexia nervosa. She has restricted intake for 9 months and lost 18 kg from a BMI of 22 to a current BMI of 14.6. Her resting heart rate is 38 /min and lying blood pressure is 88/52 mmHg. She had a syncopal episode at school yesterday. She acknowledges restriction but says she is fine.

Electrolytes show sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L, phosphate 0.68 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 478 milliseconds and no ischaemic changes. She has not menstruated in 6 months. Her parents are present and engaged. There is no overt suicidality.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 38 /min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg lying, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 35.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: BMI 14.6, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, lanugo over the back, acrocyanosis, no peripheral oedema, alert and conversing
data_table.Investigations: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.00), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), ECG sinus bradycardia QTc 478 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit directly to a child and adolescent mental health inpatient unit for psychiatric stabilisation as the sole pathway
Refer for outpatient family-based treatment with weekly weight monitoring and electrolyte review in 1 week time
Discharge with oral potassium and magnesium supplementation and review by general practitioner within 3 days
Admit to a paediatric medical ward for cardiac monitoring, electrolyte replacement and supervised structured refeeding
Commence high-calorie refeeding at 50 kcal/kg/day immediately to address the long-standing nutritional deficit fully

stem:
A 62-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium 1000 mg nocte for 12 years is brought to the emergency department by her daughter with 3 days of confusion, coarse tremor of the hands, and unsteadiness. She started ramipril 5 mg daily for newly diagnosed hypertension 10 days ago. Daughter says she has been drinking less than usual in a heatwave.

In the resus bay she is confused, has horizontal nystagmus, coarse tremor, and broad-based gait. Tendon reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus. Lithium level is 2.6 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6 to 1.0 in maintenance), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88 four months ago), sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L. ECG is in sinus rhythm with non-specific T wave flattening. She is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: confused (orientated to person only), horizontal nystagmus, coarse tremor of both hands, ankle clonus sustained, broad-based gait, no focal weakness
data_table.Investigations: lithium 2.6 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6-1.0), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88), eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m^2, sodium 142 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube to bind any unabsorbed lithium remaining in the gut lumen
Withhold lithium and commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline at 250 mL/hour with daily lithium and creatinine checks
Discuss urgent haemodialysis with the renal team and commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline at maintenance rate
Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg as a bolus to reverse the confusion and gait disturbance from suspected sedation
Stop the recently introduced ramipril and continue current lithium dose with rechecks of creatinine and level in 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Screening for occult co-ingestants after deliberate self-poisoning
stem: A 22-year-old woman presents two hours after swallowing a handful of her mother's imipramine tablets during an argument. She says she took nothing else and no alcohol. She is alert and settled and her examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/70, afebrile
data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm, QRS 88 ms, normal axis

lead_in: Which investigation is most important?

options.text: Serum paracetamol concentration at four hours
Serum tricyclic antidepressant concentration now
Urine drug screen for amphetamines and opioids
Serum ethanol concentration taken on arrival
Serum salicylate concentration at four hours

stem:
A 27-year-old long-haul truck driver presents to a community psychiatry clinic for assessment of suspected attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He has had chronic difficulties with concentration, planning, finishing tasks, and emotional regulation since primary school. He has accumulated three speeding infringements and two near-miss incidents at work in the past 18 months. The screening Adult ADHD Self Report Scale and a collateral history from his mother are highly consistent with combined-type ADHD; structured clinical interview confirms the diagnosis.

He has no history of psychosis, no current substance use disorder, no cardiac disease, blood pressure 122/78, and a normal baseline ECG. He drinks two standard drinks twice a week. He is keen to start medication so he can keep his commercial driver's licence. He has been informed that his diagnosis has driving implications.

data_table.Investigations: ECG within normal limits, blood pressure 122/78, urinary drug screen negative, full blood count and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily as a stimulant alternative with no driver licensing notification required of him
Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily and reassure him that no driver licensing notification is required at present
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone and avoid pharmacotherapy because of the commercial driving implications
Commence modafinil 100 mg daily as an off-label alternative to stimulants for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Commence dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily under psychiatry authority and notify the state driver licensing authority

stem:
A 21-year-old university student is brought to a community psychiatric assessment service by his parents with a three week history of paranoid ideation, persecutory beliefs about being followed by a state intelligence agency, and second person auditory hallucinations criticising him. He has been using high potency cannabis daily for the past four months around exam stress. He has used no other illicit substances on urine drug screen and serology.

There is no history of head injury, neurological disease, or thyroid disorder. He has a maternal uncle with chronic schizophrenia. He has stopped attending lectures and his sleep is reversed. Mental state examination shows a tense young man, suspicious, with thought disorder including loosening of associations. He has no insight. The parents say he was 'completely well' four months ago and his GP letter confirms no prior psychiatric contact.

data_table.Investigations: urine drug screen positive for cannabinoids only, full blood count within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, CRP 2 mg/L, syphilis serology negative, HIV serology negative, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain within normal limits

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose cannabis induced psychotic disorder, prescribe risperidone 1 mg twice daily for five days, discharge to GP review
Apply for an involuntary admission order under the Mental Health Act without offering voluntary admission first to him
Commence high dose oral olanzapine 20 mg daily and arrange clozapine clinic review at four weeks for resistant symptoms
Admit voluntarily under early psychosis service for trial of an oral second generation antipsychotic and substance counselling
Defer pharmacotherapy and observe abstinent in a residential rehabilitation unit for two weeks before any antipsychotic

subtopic_detail: Metabolic harm from an effective antipsychotic
stem: A 29-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder has gained 9 kg in the 12 weeks since olanzapine was started. His psychosis and mood are well controlled and he takes it reliably. He walks daily, has stopped soft drink and is distressed by the weight.

data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.8 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch olanzapine to aripiprazole
Add metformin to the olanzapine
Reduce the olanzapine dose by half
Refer to a dietitian and review later
Continue olanzapine and recheck yearly

stem:
A 56-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium 1000 mg daily for 22 years. He is psychiatrically well, has had no manic episodes in 12 years on lithium plus aripiprazole 5 mg, and is followed in shared care between psychiatry and general practice. He has hypertension on perindopril (added two years ago) and no diabetes. He drinks one glass of red wine four nights a week. His eGFR has been monitored every six months.

The most recent eGFR is 38 mL/min/1.73 m^2, falling from 54 a year ago and 72 two years ago. Lithium level today is 0.9 mmol/L. Thyroid stimulating hormone is 4.2 mU/L. Corrected calcium is 2.62 mmol/L (2.10-2.60). 24 hour urinary protein is 0.4 g (less than 0.15). He has no symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia, or tremor. The renal physician you spoke with suggested coming off lithium would not necessarily reverse the decline.

data_table.Investigations: lithium 0.9 mmol/L, eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m^2 declining from 54 then 72, thyroid stimulating hormone 4.2 mU/L, corrected calcium 2.62 mmol/L, parathyroid hormone 9.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), 24 hour urinary protein 0.4 g, blood pressure 138/82, urinary drug screen not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue lithium 1000 mg daily and recheck eGFR in six months without specialist renal medicine input
Halve the lithium dose and target a serum level of 0.4 mmol/L to reduce nephrotoxicity over the next year
Stop lithium today to halt further renal damage and substitute high dose sodium valproate from tomorrow morning
Increase fluid intake to four litres daily and continue lithium at the same dose without specialist referral
Coordinate joint psychiatry and renal medicine review for a slow lithium taper to sodium valproate or lamotrigine

stem:
A 19-year-old man with a six month prodromal history of social withdrawal and odd beliefs is brought to a psychiatric assessment unit by his family. Over the past five days he has stopped eating and drinking, has been mute, and adopts unusual postures for hours at a time. He has not been on any medication in the past year. He has no fever, no rigidity, and no autonomic instability. Vital signs are within normal limits.

On examination he is awake with eyes open but unresponsive to verbal commands. Posturing is present (he holds his arm in the air when placed there for at least 30 seconds). There is waxy flexibility on passive movement, mutism, negativism (resists eye opening), and grimacing. The remainder of the neurological examination cannot be completed due to negativism. There is no neck stiffness. Computed tomography of the brain and a metabolic screen are unremarkable.

data_table.Investigations: venous blood gas pH 7.42, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, urea 4.6 mmol/L, creatine kinase 142 U/L (<200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, urinary drug screen negative, computed tomography of the brain within normal limits, urinalysis sterile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous haloperidol 5 mg every 6 hours to treat the underlying suspected schizophrenic psychosis directly
Lorazepam 2 mg intramuscular bolus and reassess catatonic features at 15 minutes, then oral lorazepam 6 to 12 mg daily
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy under general anaesthesia without trial of pharmacotherapy as the first step
Commence intravenous flumazenil 200 micrograms to exclude benzodiazepine intoxication as a cause of unresponsiveness
Commence intravenous dantrolene 2 mg/kg to treat presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome with rigidity and autonomic signs

stem:
A 35-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 1000 mg daily for eight years with steady-state levels around 0.7 mmol/L on annual monitoring. His general practitioner prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily two weeks ago for new shoulder pain.

He now presents to a metropolitan emergency department with three days of coarse tremor, persistent nausea and vomiting, unsteady gait, and his partner reports he has become mildly confused over the last 24 hours. He has had no falls. He takes no other medications and has not started any new herbal supplements. He has continued his lithium tablets through the illness. He has no chronic kidney disease history and his last creatinine three months ago was 78 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 134/82, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: serum lithium 1.8 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 122 micromol/L (60-110), eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m squared, ECG sinus rhythm with flattened T waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop lithium and ibuprofen, commence intravenous 0.9 percent saline for volume expansion, and contact the renal team to arrange urgent haemodialysis
Continue lithium at the current dose, switch ibuprofen to paracetamol 1 g four times daily, and recheck the lithium level in 24 hours at clinic review
Reduce lithium dose to 500 mg daily, continue ibuprofen at half dose with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
Stop lithium for 48 hours then restart at 500 mg, switch mood stabiliser to sodium valproate, and continue ibuprofen as prescribed by the general practitioner
Switch lithium to a sustained release preparation and add ondansetron 8 mg three times daily for vomiting and supportive oral rehydration solution

stem:
A 28-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been taking clozapine for four weeks after two previous trials of risperidone and olanzapine with persistent psychotic symptoms. He is now on clozapine 250 mg daily with significant reduction in auditory hallucinations and improved engagement at his community clinic. He has no fever, no sore throat, no rash, and no recent infection.

He has had weekly full blood counts since starting clozapine through the registry-monitored program. His latest result today shows white cells 4.2 and absolute neutrophil count 2.0. He is asking the consultant psychiatrist what monitoring schedule applies for the next year and how it relates to his current results. He has no other medical comorbidities and takes no other medications. He understands the requirement for ongoing blood tests and is happy to comply with the schedule.

data_table.Investigations: white cells 4.2 x10^9/L (4-11), absolute neutrophil count 2.0 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), haemoglobin 142 g/L (130-180), platelets 230 x10^9/L (150-400), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), trough clozapine level 380 micrograms/L (350-600 therapeutic)

lead_in: Which monitoring schedule is correct?

options.text: Increase to twice weekly full blood count for the next four weeks given the borderline neutrophil count and continue treatment unchanged
Continue weekly full blood count until 18 weeks of clozapine, then four-weekly indefinitely while the patient remains on clozapine
Switch to monthly full blood count from week five given stable counts and good clinical response with no adverse effects in the first month
Stop clozapine immediately and switch to oral olanzapine 20 mg at night because the absolute neutrophil count is at the lower limit of normal
Continue weekly full blood count indefinitely as a routine policy for all patients prescribed clozapine throughout their treatment course

stem:
A 35-year-old man with major depressive disorder has been taking paroxetine 40 mg daily for two years. He stopped the medication five days ago without consulting his general practitioner because he felt better and thought he no longer needed it. His mood has been stable for the past six months on the medication.

He now presents to his general practitioner with five days of dizziness on standing, sensations he describes as electric brain shocks, persistent nausea, agitation, and difficulty sleeping. He denies any suicidal ideation and his mood is currently good. He has had no fever, no abdominal pain, and no new medications. He does not use alcohol or recreational drugs. His blood pressure and other observations are normal. He is keen to know what his treating doctor recommends he do next.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 84, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure him that discontinuation symptoms typically resolve spontaneously within 24 hours and continue total cessation with general supportive care
Commence fluoxetine 20 mg daily as a bridging therapy for one week and stop the fluoxetine completely without further taper
Commence venlafaxine 75 mg daily as an alternative serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor to provide ongoing maintenance therapy
Restart paroxetine 40 mg daily and then taper by twenty five percent of the dose every two to four weeks over several months
Add lorazepam 1 mg three times daily for symptomatic management of agitation and insomnia and continue paroxetine cessation

stem:
A 55-year-old woman with a recent diagnosis of severe major depressive disorder has been an inpatient for five days. The nursing staff report she has become progressively withdrawn over the last 48 hours, is now mostly mute, refuses oral intake, and lies in bed with her arm held in unusual postures.

On examination she is awake with eyes open but does not speak or respond to questions. When the resident raises her arm passively it remains in the position placed for over twenty seconds and slowly returns to the bed (waxy flexibility). She intermittently mirrors the examiner's posture. She has no fever, no rigidity, no tremor, and no autonomic instability. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score on examination is 16 (significant). She has not received any antipsychotic medication this admission and her usual antidepressants have been withheld in the last 24 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 84, blood pressure 124/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: creatine kinase 124 U/L (<200), full blood count and urea and electrolytes within normal limits, CT brain non-contrast no acute pathology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence haloperidol 5 mg intramuscular and titrate the dose to clinical response over the next twenty four hours of monitoring
Commence olanzapine 10 mg intramuscular as antipsychotic monotherapy and admit to a high dependency mental health bed for observation
Administer lorazepam 2 mg intravenously as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge and arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy if there is no response
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and increase to 100 mg over the next week with weekly review and ongoing inpatient supportive care
Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for mood stabilisation and arrange MRI brain with contrast to exclude an organic cause

subtopic_detail: Schizophreniform versus schizophrenia versus brief psychotic disorder
stem:
A 22-year-old university student is reviewed in early psychosis clinic ten weeks after his first presentation with paranoid delusions (he believed his housemates were planning to harm him) and second-person auditory hallucinations. His symptoms had been present for approximately six weeks before he was diagnosed and commenced on risperidone 2 mg at night, titrated to 4 mg.

He has been well since week four of treatment with complete resolution of delusions and hallucinations, has returned to lectures, and is functioning at his pre-illness baseline. He has had no manic or depressive episodes, no substance use, and no family history of psychotic illness on systematic enquiry. He asks his treating psychiatrist what his formal diagnosis is now that he has been well for over a month and his symptoms have completely resolved on treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 72, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: urine drug screen on initial presentation negative, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function, CT brain all within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the most likely current diagnosis?

options.text: Schizophrenia because he has had persistent psychotic symptoms with treatment and is at high risk for chronic relapsing illness
Brief psychotic disorder because his symptoms have settled rapidly with treatment and full functional recovery has been achieved
Schizoaffective disorder given the rapid response to antipsychotic treatment and complete functional restoration following the index psychotic episode
Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features given the rapid response, complete remission, and capacity to return immediately to his pre-illness baseline functioning
Schizophreniform disorder because his total symptom duration including the prodrome falls between one month and six months from index symptoms

stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with three weeks of low mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia (around eleven hours nightly), increased appetite, and a four kilogram weight gain. She denies suicidal ideation. She works as a teacher and has had to take leave.

Her psychiatric history includes an episode at age 24 where she did not sleep for two weeks, believed she was destined to start a global business empire, spent twenty thousand dollars on impulse, and was hospitalised for a fortnight. She has not been on regular psychiatric medication since then because she felt well. She has no other medical comorbidities and takes a multivitamin only. She does not use alcohol or illicit substances and her thyroid function and full blood count today are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 70, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine within normal limits, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Commence quetiapine extended release 50 mg at night and titrate to 300 mg over two weeks with general practitioner review at one and two weeks
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and titrate to 100 mg as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor monotherapy with weekly review for the first month
Commence venlafaxine 75 mg daily as a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor with general practitioner review at four weeks and at twelve weeks
Commence amitriptyline 25 mg at night for sedation and mood with titration to 75 mg over the next four weeks of close clinical review
Commence electroconvulsive therapy after four trial sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy with concurrent regular general practitioner follow up

stem:
A 27-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia has been treated with risperidone 4 mg daily for eight months with good control of psychotic symptoms and no other neuropsychiatric side effects. She has been adherent.

She now reports six months of amenorrhoea and bilateral non-bloody nipple discharge for the past three months. Pregnancy test is negative. She has no headaches or visual field changes and her body weight is stable. She is otherwise well and her psychotic symptoms remain in remission. Thyroid function and prolactin have been measured today. She has no family history of pituitary disease, no past oral contraceptive use in the last three years, and no other medications including no herbal supplements or recreational substances reported on direct questioning.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 72, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: prolactin 1850 mU/L (60-500), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), beta-hCG negative, urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue risperidone at the current dose and add cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly to lower the prolactin and restore menstruation reliably
Switch from risperidone to aripiprazole with a 2 to 4 week cross-titration and recheck prolactin and menstruation at six and twelve weeks of treatment
Continue risperidone, reduce dose to 2 mg daily, and add oral oestradiol valerate 2 mg with norethisterone for hormone replacement therapy
Arrange MRI of the pituitary urgently to exclude a prolactinoma before considering changes to her risperidone or any additional medical management
Continue risperidone unchanged and add depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg every twelve weeks for cycle suppression and bone health protection

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder attends a preconception planning appointment with her psychiatrist. She has been well for five years on lithium carbonate 1000 mg daily (level 0.7 mmol/L) after two severe manic episodes prior to commencing lithium, including one with psychotic features that required involuntary admission for six weeks.

She has tried sodium valproate previously which was ceased due to weight gain and unacceptable cognitive blunting, and a brief trial of lamotrigine alone was followed by an early manic episode within four months. She and her partner want to conceive within the next six months. She has no other medical comorbidities. Her renal function and thyroid function are normal. She understands the principles of medication monitoring and is willing to attend frequent specialist review during pregnancy if recommended.

data_table.Investigations: creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), eGFR over 90 mL/min/1.73 m squared, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-0.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue lithium throughout pregnancy at the current once daily dose with the same monitoring schedule used outside of pregnancy
Stop lithium immediately for the preconception period and reintroduce it only after delivery once breastfeeding has been weaned at six months postpartum
Continue lithium across pregnancy in divided doses with fetal cardiac ultrasound at 18 to 20 weeks and lithium level monitoring every 2 to 4 weeks
Switch lithium to sodium valproate as a first-line mood stabiliser in pregnancy planning starting now to allow for blood level stabilisation over six months
Switch lithium to lamotrigine 200 mg daily as first-line mood stabiliser through pregnancy and continue this single agent throughout the postnatal period

subtopic_detail: Clozapine + sodium valproate ineffective - calculation + failed adjunct trial
stem:
A 31-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failed adequate trials of risperidone 6 mg, olanzapine 20 mg, and paliperidone palmitate long-acting injection) has been on clozapine for 14 months, currently 425 mg at night with trough plasma clozapine 387 nanograms/mL (target range 350 to 600). He has had partial response (PANSS-positive reduction approximately 30 per cent) but continues to report distressing persistent auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions despite adherence confirmed by a community case manager and pharmacy weekly dispensing.

Sodium valproate 1000 mg BD was added three months ago for augmentation, with serum valproate trough today at 612 micromol/L (target 350 to 700 for mood-disorder dosing). His PANSS-positive score has not changed in the past 8 weeks. He has gained 4 kg, fasting glucose is now 5.9 mmol/L, and his absolute neutrophil count remains 3.8 x 10^9/L (within range).

He is not depressed, not catatonic, and has no extrapyramidal symptoms or akathisia. He has no history of self-harm or aggression. He is engaged in psychosocial rehabilitation. He has never had electroconvulsive therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Plasma clozapine 387 ng/mL (target 350-600); norclozapine 195 ng/mL; clozapine:norclozapine ratio 1.98; ANC 3.8 x 10^9/L; fasting glucose 5.9 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.4%; lipids within normal limits; weight gain 4 kg over 3 months
data_table.Examination: No EPS, no akathisia, no orthostatic hypotension; AIMS score 0
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 425 mg nocte; sodium valproate 1000 mg BD; no other psychotropic; smoker 10 cigarettes/day

lead_in: Which one of the following augmentation strategies has the strongest evidence for partial-response clozapine-treated schizophrenia in this patient?

options.text: Add a course of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) of 8 to 12 sessions twice weekly, continue clozapine, and review response at 4 weeks of ECT before further escalation
Increase clozapine to 525 mg nocte with re-checked trough level at 1 week, smoking cessation counselling, and review of clinical response at 6 weeks
Add aripiprazole 5 mg daily titrated to 15 mg over 4 weeks as antipsychotic augmentation of clozapine, with continuous metabolic monitoring
Cease sodium valproate, commence lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated to 200 mg over 6 weeks as a clozapine adjunct, and review response at 12 weeks
Continue clozapine and valproate at current doses, optimise psychosocial rehabilitation including cognitive behaviour therapy for psychosis, and review at 12 weeks
